China Might Lap the United States on AI Adoption. Beijing’s collaborative approach is winning over other states.
IMF Chief Issues Stark Economic Warning for 2027. Kristalina Georgieva urges world leaders to implement protective measures to help keep the lights on.
Pakistan’s Opposition on the March. Simmering anger over former leader Imran Khan’s imprisonment drives protesters back to the streets—and toward Islamabad.
The Leverage Middle Powers Have in the AI Race. Allied democracies can offer something U.S. industry desperately needs.
America’s Best Answer to the China-Russia Alliance. Washington can exploit friction, strengthen allies, and make the axis harder to sustain.
The Real Danger May Be AI as Dumb as Us. Talk of “super intelligence” distracts from frequent screwups.
Can a New Credit Rating Agency Help Africans Borrow at Better Rates?. The African Union is challenging the big three rating agencies’ approach to assessing African borrowing risk.
Where the Saudi-Houthi War Stands Now. The Yemeni rebel forces ramp up strikes on Saudi airports, oil refineries, and other critical infrastructure.
To Understand France’s Unrest, Look Back to 1982. François Mitterrand’s U-turn decades ago holds lessons for today.
The Next Iran War Is This Iran War. The Iran war is, and always was, about regime change.
Trump Is Reopening the Middle East’s Deadliest Sectarian Fault Lines. Washington is pressing Shiite groups to disarm while ignoring the real fears that keep them armed.
How America and China Compare on AI. And why the two countries have different definitions of winning.
Mecca Pact, Activated. What Pakistan and Turkey will likely do (and want) in Saudi Arabia.
Brazil’s Far-Right Resurgence. The Bolsonaro family looks likely to retake the presidency.

Iran workers face delayed wages, lost benefits and job fears. Workers across several sectors in Iran say employers are delaying or splitting wage payments, cutting benefits and warning staff they could lose their jobs for protesting, as inflation and rising living costs deepen pressure on households.

Iran escalates Starlink threats over fears of losing internet control. Iranian authorities have stepped up warnings against Starlink as the cost-of-living crisis deepens and the prospect of renewed public protests grows, signaling mounting concern over citizens’ access to satellite internet.

Two more January protesters executed in Iran. The Islamic Republic executed two more people detained in connection with the January 2026 protests, bringing to seven the number put to death in the Alikhani Square case in Isfahan, rights groups and the judiciary reported Monday.

Netanyahu predicts Iran regime’s fall, Tehran warns war could engulf region. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu predicted the eventual fall of Iran’s leadership while the Islamic Republic’s top armed forces commander warned a new conflict would engulf the region, sharpening exchanges over the prospect of renewed fighting on Monday.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate defense pact over Houthi attacks. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activated collective deterrence measures Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy forces and military capabilities to the kingdom, as Saudi-backed Yemeni troops advanced against the Iran-backed Houthis.

Pezeshkian nominates missile-industry veteran as defense minister. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as defense minister, moving to fill a post left vacant since Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed in US-Israeli strikes in February.

Iran says US talks ‘meaningless’ as third tanker hit near Hormuz. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that talks with the United States were meaningless, even as President Donald Trump remained open to direct negotiations, while a third tanker in two days was struck near the Strait of Hormuz.

IRGC commander says his wife founded Minab school hit in February strike. The school struck in February in Iran’s Minab was founded by the wife of senior IRGC commander Ali Fadavi as part of a wider educational project linked to the Guards’ navy, according to his remarks and an earlier Iranian media account.

IRGC commander, son helped build new oil-sales network. Senior IRGC commander Hossein-Reza Sadeghi and his son Saeed played central roles in efforts to preserve an IRGC Intelligence oil-sales network and shift its financial operations from the United Arab Emirates to Russia, an Iran International investigation found.

Why Iran’s oil minister quit at a critical moment for exports. Iran’s oil minister left office as exports fell sharply and questions mounted over billions of dollars in sanctioned crude sales, bringing disputes over oil intermediaries, corporate management and political pressure into focus.

Iran sentences 38-year-old to death as January protest executions mount. Hadi Abbasian, a 38-year-old resident of northeastern Iran, has been sentenced to death by a Revolutionary Court in Bojnurd after being arrested over his support for the nationwide protests in January, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Iran releases cleric who called for replacing Islamic Republic on bail. Iranian authorities have released hardline cleric Mohammad-Bagher Kharrazi on bail after about a month in detention, the judiciary said on Tuesday.

Clothes, diaries, dolls: Iran forces raid slain protesters’ rooms. Clothes, diaries, books and childhood dolls are being taken from the bedrooms of protesters killed in Iran, as security forces extend pressure on families seeking accountability into the most private spaces of their grief nearly nine months after the January 2026 killings.

Tehran police warn cafes over live music, DJs and hookah. Police in Tehran have warned cafes that they could face closure or lose their licenses for hosting live music, using DJs or serving hookah, extending a broader campaign of enforcement against businesses over entertainment, mandatory hijab rules and support for protests.

Houthi gains reversed at Bab al-Mandab, but Iran’s leverage runs deeper. Saudi-backed Yemeni forces on Monday reversed weeks of Houthi gains around Bab al-Mandab, the strategic strait linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, exposing vulnerabilities in the Iran-backed group even as fighting elsewhere showed how far Yemen remains from a decisive shift.

Iranians cross into Armenia to earn what they cannot at home. Economic crisis is driving some Iranians across the border to Armenia for construction, taxi and delivery work, turning a longtime holiday destination into a source of income for families struggling to make ends meet at home.

Three Iranians spied on Iran International journalists in UK, prosecutors say. Three Iranian men spied on Iran International journalists to assist Iranian intelligence services and prepare for serious violence against at least one target, prosecutors told a London court Tuesday.

Iran, US back to ‘square one’ as diplomacy stalls. Rhetoric is hardening on both sides of the Iran-US standoff, with even Iranian analysts traditionally optimistic about diplomacy warning that relations are slipping back to “square one” as military and economic pressure intensifies.

Iran executes nearly two people a week since January protests. Iran has executed nearly two people a week in political and security cases since the January protests, including over protest- and war-related accusations, while another 194 people face death sentences, an Iran International review of cases shows.

‘Hugging actors are married’: Tehran theatre navigates contact restrictions. A theater production in Tehran displayed a notice to spectators before a performance saying two actors who embrace on stage are married, underscoring the restrictions governing physical contact between men and women under the Islamic Republic.

‘Let ’em take out Los Angeles’: Trump’s Iran remarks ignite backlash. President Donald Trump’s suggestion that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego has sparked a backlash from California officials and prompted the White House to insist that he was misunderstood as he defended the mounting costs of the war with Tehran.

How Iran’s 2022 crackdown was coordinated from the top. Iran’s repression of the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising was coordinated from the top through a functioning chain of command linking senior authorities to security forces on the streets, Amnesty International says.

Iran says economy holding up as pressure mounts on oil, rial. Iran’s central bank chief has rejected what he portrays as a US prediction of economic collapse, even as the rial trades near record lows and Iranian oil exports have fallen to zero.

Iran’s own surveys reveal demand for 'fundamental change'. Two surveys emerging from within or around Iran's political establishment paint a bleak picture of public confidence: deep skepticism toward state institutions, single-digit trust in political officials and overwhelming demand for change.

Iran lawmaker named in alleged illegal treasure excavation. A senior hardline Iranian lawmaker has been named in an allegation involving unauthorized excavation for antiquities and treasure, while parliament is also examining a reported excavation case involving an unnamed member of the legislature.

Family of executed January protester says Iran concealed burial site. The family of Alireza Raisi, executed this week over the January protests in Isfahan, still does not know where he was buried after security agents took his father blindfolded to the burial site, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iran protester recounts torture, mock execution after January arrest. “Write your will.” Those were the words Iranian protester Erfan Nabian says he heard in solitary confinement before he was handed a sheet of paper and asked what he wanted for his final meal before his execution.

Parsian Exchange transferred millions of dollars for Iran despite sanctions. Iran’s Bank Parsian, under US sanctions, used its foreign-exchange arm to move millions of dollars abroad through a network of intermediaries, according to an Iran International investigation based on leaked internal correspondence and transaction records.

Rubio says Iran missed deal chances as Tehran digs in on enrichment. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran had failed to take advantage of repeated opportunities to reach an agreement with Washington over its nuclear program, while also saying Tehran had “lost complete control” of the Strait of Hormuz.

Tehran divided over $2 billion plan to prop up rial. Iran’s central bank is offering as much as $2 billion in cash dollars to the public in an effort to slow the rial’s slide, triggering a fierce debate over whether the intervention can stabilize the currency or merely burn through increasingly scarce foreign reserves.

China shifts to Iraqi oil: is Iran using old workaround to beat US blockade?. China’s independent refiners are turning to Iraqi crude to replace dwindling Iranian supplies as a US blockade chokes Tehran’s exports, raising questions about whether Iran is using an old workaround to reach its buyers: disguising its own oil as Iraqi.

Kayhan attacks Ghalibaf’s role in talks. Didn’t Khamenei approve it?. An editorial questioning Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf’s role as Iran’s lead negotiator has raised an awkward question in Tehran: who exactly is Kayhan criticizing, given that senior officials have said the parliament speaker was given the job with the Supreme Leader’s approval?

‘$100k-a-month captains’: What it costs to move oil through Hormuz. Oil tanker captains are being paid as much as $100,000 a month and offered $50,000 bonuses for individual trips through the Strait of Hormuz, the latest sign of the extraordinary costs now required to keep crude moving through the waterway since the Iran war began.

Iran looks for escape routes as US sanctions close in. The widening reach of US sanctions across Iran’s transport and industrial networks has raised alarms in Tehran that Washington is seeking to close off the alternative trade routes the country has relied on to circumvent years of economic pressure.

From talks to war: Tehran sees the gap narrowing. Fears of renewed war with the United States, Israel or both are growing in Iran, as military officials talk openly about pre-emptive action and analysts warn that the distance between diplomacy and another round of fighting is becoming dangerously short.

Hezbollah recruitment network in Iran exposed, four safe houses identified. Hezbollah’s external operations unit has been recruiting foreign nationals in Iran and using safe houses in Qom and Tehran to train and shelter recruits, according to information obtained by Iran International.

Islamic Republic supporters take weapons home after training, citizens say. Some participants in military training programs for supporters of the Islamic Republic, including Basij militia members and seminary students, have been allowed to take weapons home, citizens told Iran International, as authorities expand firearms training to schools across Iran.

Police officer killed in armed attack near Zahedan as violence continues in southeast Iran. An Iranian police officer was killed on Thursday when gunmen attacked a patrol near Zahedan in Sistan-Baluchestan, the latest in a series of deadly attacks and clashes involving security forces in southeastern Iran.

Iran's reported $200 million Hezbollah aid angers cash-strapped citizens. Reports that the Islamic Republic sent $200 million to Lebanon's Hezbollah have drawn anger from Iranians struggling with rising living costs, low wages and medicine shortages, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Three years after October 7, Iran pays the price of miscalculation. Three years after Hamas's October 7 attack on Israel, the Islamic Republic faces a weakened network of regional allies, direct military confrontation and mounting economic pressure, upending its long-held strategy of deterring enemies while keeping war away from its territory.

US sanctions 17 ships in push to shut down Iran’s shadow fleet. The US Treasury sanctioned 17 vessels and their owners Thursday under Operation Economic Outcast, saying the action effectively neutralizes most of Iran’s remaining shadow fleet.

Saudi Aramco hires US firm to upgrade shared oil field as Iran lags behind. Saudi Aramco has hired a US engineering firm to upgrade an offshore oil field it shares with Iran, which has fallen far behind several neighbors in developing shared energy reserves.

Trump rules out Iran attack before midterms, Tehran says ready for prolonged war. US President Donald Trump said Thursday the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that "productive" talks were underway, after reports of US preparations for possible large-scale strikes.

US pressure hits Iranians harder than rulers, 68% in poll say. More than two-thirds of respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll said the Trump administration’s pressure on the Islamic Republic is hurting ordinary Iranians more than the authorities.

Taliban-run Afghanistan could get ‘land of its own’ on Iran’s coast, MP says. Iran has reached a preliminary understanding to allocate land at Chabahar to Taliban-run Afghanistan to build infrastructure for moving its goods to the sea, an Iranian lawmaker said.

Iraq creates PMF unit to take faction drones as arms plan advances - Erem News. Iraq has created a specialized unit within the Popular Mobilization Forces to take control of drones held by armed factions as part of Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s plan to bring weapons under state authority, Erem News reported on Friday, citing an Iraqi security source.

At least five members of Iranian forces killed in four southeast attacks - Haalvsh. At least five Iranian military and police personnel were killed and several others wounded in four armed attacks across southeastern Iran within 24 hours, Haalvsh reported, as violence targeting security forces continued across the area.

Iran-origin campaign targeted Iran International, foreign media - OpenAI. An Iran-origin influence operation used fake Western journalist identities to place nearly 100 articles in online news outlets around the world and repeatedly generated hostile social media responses to Iran International, OpenAI said in a report released on Thursday.

Two men deny spying for Iran on Israeli embassy in London. Two men accused of carrying out surveillance on the Israeli Embassy, Britain’s oldest synagogue and other Jewish and Israeli-linked sites in London on behalf of Iran pleaded not guilty on Friday.

UK court hears how alleged Iran spy operation targeted Iran International. Men accused of spying for Iran exchanged information about Iran International’s offices and presenter Kambiz Hosseini, while one defendant discussed money transfers and his legal troubles with contacts in Iran, a London court heard.

Côte d’Ivoire : comment l’opposition s’est entendue, en coulisses, sur la nouvelle CEI. Au terme de trois jours de négociations, quatre groupements de partis d’opposition se sont accordés, pour la première fois depuis longtemps, sur une proposition à présenter au gouvernement au sujet du nouvel organe électoral. Sauf que le PPA-CI, de Laurent Gbagbo, pourtant signataire, a brillé par son absence…

Bénin-France : ce qu’il faut retenir de la rencontre entre Romuald Wadagni et Emmanuel Macron. Le chef de l’État béninois a effectué sa première visite officielle en France, où il a scellé trois accords économiques avec son homologue. Et, selon nos informations, acté la nomination de l’ancien ministre de la Culture Jean-Michel Abimbola comme futur ambassadeur à Paris.

RDC – Guylain Nyembo : « Le recensement couvrira tout le territoire national ». Quarante-deux ans après le dernier recensement national, le gouvernement congolais relance cet immense chantier dans un contexte de tensions politiques et sécuritaires. Autant d’obstacles que le ministre du Plan affirme pouvoir surmonter.

Finale de la CAN 2025 entre le Maroc et le Sénégal : une troisième mi-temps devant le Tribunal arbitral du sport. Le Sénégal, le Maroc et la CAF plaideront ce jeudi devant l’instance d’arbitrage de Lausanne. Objectif : trancher enfin le litige né de la finale de la dernière CAN, alors que le titre n’a toujours pas été réattribué, près d’un an après le match qui a mis le feu aux poudres.

Au Cameroun, les coulisses de la levée de la suspension de Vision 4 par René Emmanuel Sadi. Suspendue par le Conseil national de la communication le 29 septembre, la chaîne de télévision a retrouvé les ondes le 5 octobre, à la demande du ministre de la Communication et de la présidence et de la République. Le CNC est fragilisé.

Maroc : ce que la rupture Algérie-Émirats arabes unis change pour Rabat. Pris entre un allié émirati de plus en plus offensif et une Algérie déterminée à reprendre toute sa place dans le Sahel, le Maroc se retrouve au cœur d’un jeu régional qui se tend. La rupture entre Alger et Abou Dhabi pourrait rebattre bien plus de cartes qu’il n’y paraît.

Le port de Dakar peut-il garder son avance face à la concurrence régionale ?. À peine installé à la direction du Port autonome de Dakar (PAD), Doune Pathé Mbengue donne le ton. Modernisation, numérisation, connexion aux réseaux routier et ferroviaire… Face à Abidjan notamment, Dakar a fort à faire pour conserver son rang de port à conteneurs le plus performant d’Afrique subsaharienne.

Niger : disparu depuis août, le journaliste Moussa Kaka est « détenu » par les autorités. La junte menée par Abdourahamane Tiani reprocherait au directeur de la chaîne RTS, et ancien correspondant de RFI, d’avoir « commis une infraction », sans préciser laquelle, et a annoncé qu’il devrait « répondre devant les juridictions ».

Minerais critiques : la RDC mise sur la cartographie de son sous-sol pour séduire les investisseurs. Dans un contexte de transition énergétique et de lutte d’influence entre la Chine et les États-Unis, Kinshasa veut mieux connaître l’étendue de la richesse de son sous-sol en minerais critiques. Un prérequis pour « mieux défendre les intérêts du pays ».

Mohamed Rabie Khlie, le patron de l’ONCF chargé de mettre le Maroc sur les rails du Mondial 2030. Sous la houlette de l’ingénieur de 63 ans, l’Office national des chemins de fer a réussi à moderniser et à étendre le réseau ferroviaire du royaume. Mais au prix d’un équilibre financier précaire et de retards dans sa mue en société anonyme.

Affaire Kemi Seba : la justice sud-africaine rouvre la voie à une extradition vers le Bénin. Incarcéré en Afrique du Sud, l’activiste visé par une extradition vers le Bénin s’est vu refuser la protection diplomatique. Un revers majeur pour sa défense, qui mise désormais sur l’audience prévue en novembre.

Loi anticorruption en RDC : Guillaume Ngefa a-t-il les moyens de ses ambitions ?. Présenté le 28 septembre à l’Assemblée nationale, le projet de loi porté par le ministre de la Justice promet de moderniser la lutte contre la corruption. Reste à savoir s’il pourra réussir dans un domaine où son prédécesseur avait lui-même promis d’agir.

Pourquoi la vente d’Oragroup est devenue une course contre la montre vitale. En quête d’une recapitalisation cruciale, le groupe bancaire panafricain a réuni son conseil d’administration le 7 octobre. En vente depuis 2019, la banque est contrainte de réduire ses octrois de crédits pour assurer sa survie.

Prétoires, pouvoir et réseaux : ces avocats qui façonnent la politique ivoirienne. Habiba Touré, Jean-Chrysostome Blessy, Abdoulaye Meïté… En Côte d’Ivoire, les robes noires s’imposent au premier rang des batailles de partis, au sein desquels ils sont militants ou responsables. Le Palais de justice d’Abidjan est ainsi devenu le nouveau théâtre des luttes de pouvoir.

Présidentielle au Cameroun : quand Anicet Ekane attendait Issa Tchiroma Bakary à Yaoundé. En octobre 2025, l’activiste aujourd’hui décédé a été l’un des principaux soutiens du candidat à la présidentielle. Pourtant, leur alliance face à Paul Biya ne s’est pas déroulée comme prévu.

L’Égypte parviendra-t-elle à contenir l’Éthiopie ?. Le Caire tente de rassembler autour de lui les adversaires de l’Éthiopie, mais on ignore encore quelle est la solidité de l’alliance qu’il a nouée avec l’Érythrée, le Soudan et la Somalie, et quelle sera la réaction de Washington.

Hôtellerie : au Sahel, les acteurs se réinventent sans les ONG ni la clientèle étrangère. Privés d’une partie de leur clientèle internationale par la crise sécuritaire et le recul de l’aide au développement, les hôtels sahéliens repensent leurs offres. De Bamako à Ouagadougou, ils tentent de séduire la clientèle locale.

« C’est le moment de rendre les armes » : à Bissau, le général N’Tam lance un appel aux militaires restés proches d’Embaló. Après l’annonce de la candidature à la présidentielle du président déchu Umaro Sissoco Embaló, se sont ensuivies des rumeurs de mécontentement au sein de la garde présidentielle. Dans la foulée, plusieurs éléments ont été désarmés et placés sous contrôle de l’état-major.

Burkina Faso : 10 choses à savoir sur le général Diaouari, le maître à penser sécuritaire d’Ibrahim Traoré. Très proche du président burkinabè, qui l’a élevé au rang de général en juillet dernier, cet officier au profil de technocrate est devenu central dans le dispositif d’Ibrahim Traoré. Des questions sécuritaires à la communication, en passant par la mise en œuvre du souverainisme économique, il est l’un des stratèges de la junte.

Sénégal : le calendrier de la restructuration de la dette est-il crédible ?. Dakar vise un premier soutien du FMI dès le mois de novembre avant de boucler un accord sur sa dette avec les créanciers en décembre. Mais le calendrier semble particulièrement serré.

Le Maroc, porte d’entrée des industries de défense émiraties sur le continent. La présence massive des fournisseurs émiratis de matériel militaire au Marrakech Air Show n’est qu’une manifestation d’un phénomène plus large. Pour Abou Dhabi, le Maroc est plus qu’un marché, c’est aussi un pays stratégique pour séduire les armées de tout le continent.

RDC : Félix Tshisekedi sollicite l’aide de la Monusco pour la démobilisation des FDLR. Le président congolais a écrit au secrétaire général des Nations unies pour qu’il soutienne son plan de démobilisation des anciens génocidaires hutu. La proposition pourrait être étudiée dans le cadre du renouvellement du mandat de la Monusco.

Pour Airtel Money, l’entrée en Bourse est aussi un moyen de relancer les acquisitions. Valorisé 7 milliards de dollars, le géant de la finance mobile s’apprête à faire son entrée à la Bourse de Londres. Elle offre au groupe une vitrine boursière pour mener la consolidation de la fintech en Afrique et convertir ses 75 millions de clients télécoms.

Saddam Haftar : du Sahel au Tchad, les limites d’une diplomatie sécuritaire. Entre libérations d’otages, soutien à des mouvements rebelles et nouvelle alliance avec le Tchad, l’héritier du maréchal Haftar cherche à s’imposer comme un interlocuteur incontournable. Et se rêve en futur président d’une Libye réunifiée qui pèserait de nouveau sur la diplomatie continentale.

Au Cameroun, Maurice Kamto tente la stratégie de l’éminence grise. Alors que le MRC s’apprête à désigner son successeur lors d’une convention toujours contestée, l’opposant reste présent en coulisses. En retrait, il travaille à l’implantation nationale du parti et veut peser sur ses futures alliances électorales.

Pétrole : les dessous de l’incursion manquée de Simon Tiemtoré dans l’aval africain. Le banquier américano-burkinabé s’était positionné, via Lilium Capital Group, pour l’acquisition d’un réseau de quelque 400 stations-service. Mais les discussions n’ont finalement pas abouti. Coulisses.

Le prix Nobel de la paix décerné à la juriste sud-africaine Navanethem « Navi » Pillay. Le prix Nobel de la paix a été décerné, ce vendredi 9 octobre, à la juriste sud-africaine Navi Pillay, qui a notamment présidé la commission d’enquête de l’ONU ayant accusé Israël de commettre un « génocide » à Gaza.

James Mwangi (Equity) : « L’Afrique doit ajouter de la valeur à ce qu’elle produit ». Expansion régionale, IA et projet de raffinerie à Lamu : le patron du groupe kényan Equity, leader en Afrique de l’Est, met en avant sa stratégie pour assurer l’essor et la diversification de ses activités. Tout en insistant sur la nécessité pour le continent de mieux maîtriser ses chaînes de valeur.

Détention d’Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze au Gabon : les coulisses d’un dossier sensible. L’ancien Premier ministre et opposant au président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema est toujours incarcéré à la prison centrale de Libreville dans l’attente de son procès. Ses conseils fustigent une procédure judiciaire gelée et dénoncent une arrestation politique, ce que réfutent les autorités.

Maroc : avant le discours du roi, où en sont les négociations pour former une coalition ?. Les tractations conduites par Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri dessinent les contours possibles d’une majorité articulée autour du PAM et des trois partis historiques de la Koutla. Mais les consultations se poursuivent et d’autres options restent ouvertes.

Ebola : le Kenya confirme son tout premier mort. Un Kényan vivant en République démocratique du Congo est mort de la maladie à virus Ebola, lundi 5 octobre, dans un hôpital de Nairobi, a annoncé le ministre de la santé kényan. Il s’agit du premier décès lié à cette maladie jamais recensé dans ce pays d’Afrique de l’Est.

Cheikh Hamidou Kane, écrivain et acteur de la construction d’un Sénégal indépendant, est mort. Ecrivain mais aussi homme d’Etat, plusieurs fois ministre, il était à la fois témoin et acteur de l’histoire contemporaine du Sénégal. Cheikh Hamidou Kane est mort le 3 octobre à Dakar, à l’âge de 98 ans.

Génocide des Tutsi au Rwanda : « Le non-lieu à l’encontre des militaires français à Bisesero n’a pas de valeur historique ». La Cour de cassation a définitivement confirmé, début septembre, le non-lieu prononcé en appel à l’égard de cinq militaires français jugés pour « complicité de génocide » au Rwanda en 1994. L’historien Vincent Duclert revient, dans un entretien au « Monde », sur cette décision.

Au Sénégal, les promesses non tenues de l’exploitation pétrolière et gazière. Le pays a découvert des gisements prometteurs en 2014, mais les investissements étrangers n’ont pas suffi à apporter des bénéfices importants. Deux contrats récemment signés témoignent d’une reprise des projets, au ralenti ces dernières années.

Dans la Somalie en guerre, une aide humanitaire empêchée, des populations menacées de famine. Les violents combats entre factions gouvernementales rivales aggravent encore la crise alimentaire qui touche près de sept millions de Somaliens. Fuyant la sécheresse et la faim, les réfugiés ne cessent d’affluer dans les camps où se trouvent les organisations humanitaires, bannies de certaines zones par le mouvement islamiste chabab.

Au Mali, l’armée signe une rare victoire après la prise de la ville stratégique de Kidal, désertée par les rebelles. Cette annonce de la reprise de cette ville devenue un bastion de la rébellion touareg intervient après une série de revers pour l’armée malienne.

Au Mali, la junte regagne du terrain en reprenant Kidal, fief des rebelles touareg. Les militaires maliens et leurs alliés russes avaient été chassés de la ville du Nord le 25 avril, durant l’offensive conjointe des indépendantistes du Front de libération de l’Azawad et des djihadistes du Groupe de soutien de l’islam et des musulmans.

Le journaliste nigérien Moussa Kaka est « en vie » et « détenu » par les autorités, selon Reporters sans frontières. Le sort du journaliste, directeur d’une télévision privée, suscitait de nombreuses inquiétudes depuis sa disparition, le 31 août.

« La France doit accorder l’asile au lanceur d’alerte et journaliste Ephrem Yalike-Ngonzo ». Dans une tribune au « Monde », Reporters sans frontières, le réseau Forbidden Stories et la Plateforme de protection des lanceurs d’alerte en Afrique exhortent les autorités françaises à octroyer l’asile au journaliste centrafricain, source exclusive d’une enquête sur la machine de propagande russe en Afrique.

Des troupes érythréennes sont entrées en Ethiopie, laissant craindre un affrontement direct avec Addis-Abeba. L’armée d’Asmara soutient les insurgés du Front populaire de libération du Tigré, en lutte contre le gouvernement central éthiopien. Des camions militaires et des équipements lourds érythréens ont été aperçus sur le territoire éthiopien.

French student protests: A generation that sees no future is rising up Submitted by Alain Gabon on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 16:20 Trump has wrongly tried to blame the student-led movement on migrants and Islam. In reality, it is propelled by the gradual disappearance of any prospect of a stable future A placard reads "The youth shouts, the state brings out its weapons" during a student protest in eastern France, on 8 October 2026 (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP) Off Since late September, France has lived to the tempo of massive high school student protests and blockades , culminating this week in a nationwide demonstration that brought out hundreds of thousands of people across the country. Originating in a low-income suburb of Paris , the movement spread like wildfire across France, quickly expanding to encompass university students and union activists. While the movement is mostly made up of teenagers who have overwhelmingly remained peaceful, state authorities have responded with disproportionate force . Rather than insisting on moderation, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called for police to use the full range of intermediate weapons , such as tear gas and rubber bullets, as necessary on protesters. More than 6,000 people , mostly minors, have been arrested in the crackdown. Predictably, since day one, the mainstream media has worked hand-in-hand with the Macron government to discredit the movement, showing almost exclusively the more sensationalist, scary and spectacular images from the protests. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The coverage aims to create the false impression that “France is burning”, presenting the protests as “violent riots”, rather than as a largely peaceful student movement with legitimate and reasonable demands. Deliberately ignored in such coverage is the fact that the vast majority of the countless protests, blockades, marches and actions in recent days, including the massive nationwide demonstration this week, remained non-violent. Media coverage has also portrayed the students as being manipulated or instrumentalised by the France Unbowed party and its leader, Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is running in next year’s presidential election. They have presented no evidence for this claim, beyond the party’s support for the youth movement. Enter Trump Beating the French media and politicians - from the centre left to the far right - at their own Islamophobic and racist games, US President Donald Trump recently weighed in by publicly blaming the protests on uncontrolled mass migration and Islam. Such outlandish accusations hardly deserve a response, and in France, they have essentially been ignored as the ravings of a despicable lunatic. Students complain about severe underfunding of the public education system, even as the state spends billions of dollars in subsidies on private, usually Catholic schools There are, however, two other explanations. Trump and others in his entourage might genuinely believe in the Great Replacement fantasy that “European civilisation” is being eclipsed by Muslims and Arabs, who want to build some sort of “Islamist caliphate”. Alternatively, he might simply be playing to his largely xenophobic Maga base, ahead of November midterms that his party is poised to lose . But Trump’s grotesque posturing as a defender of “western civilisation” against invading hordes from the Global South does not seem to have swayed many people, even in the US, likely because few American voters have much interest in the politics of France. The reasons for the protests are much simpler than Trump suggests. They have been abundantly, even relentlessly, explained by the students themselves , as well as by some good, honest reporting and expert commentary . Despite vast disparities across the nation, the primary grievances of students include the often appalling physical conditions of their crumbling schools; severe and systematic shortages of teachers and support staff; and overcrowded classrooms, where the numbers of students sometimes exceed available chairs. In general, students complain about severe underfunding and governmental neglect of the public education system, even as the state spends billions of dollars in subsidies on private, usually Catholic schools - a cruel irony for a supposedly secular state whose elected officials constantly brag about the strictness of French laicite. Restless generation Another reason cited by student protesters is the strong and mounting anxiety they feel about their prospects for the future. This deep-seated fear crystallises around a state-run web portal called “ Parcoursup ”, which launched in 2018 with a goal of sorting out university applications. Widely viewed as a failure, the automated selection system pits students against other students for their choice of universities and specialisations, in a process that has been criticised as opaque and discriminatory. France riots: Why the streets are burning again Read More » While France legally guarantees postsecondary access for students who have completed high school, 320,000 students were left without a place last year by the Parcoursup platform. In a nation of just 2.26 million high school students , many of whom will not even apply for higher education, the ratio is worrying. And this is just the tip of the iceberg. History shows that behind concrete, practical and material demands, and beyond massive and spectacular popular demonstrations, larger problems often loom. What we are hearing in France is an expression of generalised anxiety over the future, both individually and globally, and a rejection of the state of affairs at home after a decade of disastrous Macronism, which has broken the country and greatly aggravated inequalities, deepening the divide between rich and poor, and thrusting most of the population into ever-worsening precarity. Researchers have suggested that young people in Generation Z will be worse off than their parents, facing a more difficult path to adulthood than any generation in half a century. Such is the future many of these student protesters see in front of them. Add to this their emerging awareness that AI is killing and replacing many of the jobs that were supposed to be theirs, and there is no need to see the hands of shadowy “Islamists” behind this historic movement. Navi Pillay, eminent South African jurist, awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize Submitted by Sondos Asem on Fri, 10/09/2026 - 10:28 Pillay was the chair of the UN committee that concluded last year that Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza, and is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice Former United Nations rights chief Navi Pillay pictured in Johannesburg in 2023 (Wikus de Wet/AFP) Off Navi Pillay, the eminent South African jurist who co-authored the United Nations report accusing Israel of committing genocide in Gaza , has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced on Friday. The committee said Pillay had been chosen "for her efforts to promote peace and international law". "The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted," the committee said. Pillay, 85, is one of the most influential figures in international criminal justice and human rights law, and is South Africa’s most prominent international judge. In her first reaction to the announcement, Pillay noted her last work as the the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded in an authoritative report last year that Israel is responsible for genocide in Gaza . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "The last thing I did is the report on Gaza naming what is happening there as genocide," she told a gathering of friends and colleagues at courtroom 600 at the Nuremberg Palace of Justice in Germany. "One of the main reactions to that report [was] paying tribute to me for my courage.. why would you need courage to speak the truth?" she said at the historic venue which hosted the post-World War II war crimes trials of the Nazis. A former UN high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014, Pillay was nominated by Nelson Mandela, then the president of South Africa, in 1995 to serve on the UN's International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), where she served as a judge and president (1999-2003). Pillay's work at the ICTR produced the first genocide convictions in history. She was also one of the founding judges of the International Criminal Court, and currently serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is due to determine whether the Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. As the president of the ICTR, Pillay helped establish that rape and sexual violence can constitute genocide, setting a historic precedent in the jurisprudence on genocide. In a wide-ranging interview with Middle East Eye's Expert Witness podcast last year, Pillay said that as a UN expert investigating genocide in Gaza she found "a lot of similarities" with her previous work on sexual violence as a form of genocide. Exclusive: Navi Pillay on Israel's Gaza genocide and global complicity Read More » "The commission finds a lot of similarities in the Akayesu case and what is currently unfolding in Gaza," she told MEE, referring to the landmark ICTR case that delivered the first conviction where rape was recognised as an act of genocide. "We found that the widespread and gender-based violence was instrumentalised, not only as punishment against the individuals, but as part of a pattern of collective punishment to fracture, humiliate, and subjugate the Palestinian population in its entirety," she said. "I was recognised for having delivered that first judgment and for writing that portion of it. That jurisprudence is directly applicable to the Gaza situation." The Nobel prize committee recognised Pillay's work at the UN commission, as well as her contribution to setting precedents at international court cases. "History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges - those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos - are therefore highly deserving of our praise," said the committee. "But today, as these same judges are sanctioned , and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination - qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench." 'No one listens to us': France's mass student protests expose social and racial inequality Submitted by Pauline Ertel on Thu, 10/08/2026 - 01:02 Students from disadvantaged suburbs demand better conditions and equal opportunities in a system that has neglected their communities Protesters during a blockade of Sciences Po university in Paris as part of nationwide protests demanding better school conditions in France, 7 October 2026 (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters) Off As France 's student protests stretch into a third week, testimonies from young people show how unequal and often degrading school conditions fall hardest on ethnic minorities and working‑class suburbs. Police violence has intensified and schools have been disrupted nationwide, pushing students from the banlieues – France ’s working‑class, often ethnically diverse suburbs – to demand better conditions and an end to the structural inequalities they say marginalise their communities. The protests began in mid-September following a staff and students strike over teacher shortages and deteriorating conditions at the Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, in the southeastern suburb of Paris. When videos of the strike circulated online, other high schools joined in, blocking entrances and staging demonstrations. Within 10 days, the movement had spread nationwide. According to figures from the interior ministry, by 6 October around 250,000 people - including school and university students, parents, teachers and unionists - had taken to the streets to demand higher public investment in education and improved conditions, particularly in low‑income neighbourhoods. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Their demands range from renovated facilities and increased staffing to smaller class sizes, a fairer college application system and an alternative to the current “8h-18h” school day. The French state has reacted with what rights groups, including Amnesty International , have condemned as an "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force, urging authorities to de-escalate. Footage circulating online shows police and national guard units deploying tear gas, firing rubber bullets and beating protesters with batons. Hundreds have been injured, some very seriously. In Val‑d’Oise, a 14‑year‑old lost several teeth after a tear‑gas canister was fired at his face at point‑blank range. In Lens, a 15-year old student lost his hand in a confrontation with police. Following the incident, the interior minister announced a temporary halt on stun grenades at school demonstrations, while rejecting accusations of police brutality. Meanwhile, more than 5,000 protestors have been arrested - 85 percent of them minors, according to the ministry. Dilapidated schools The wave of high‑school blockades across the country has exposed a deep crisis in the education system. Material conditions are a central grievance. In many high schools, particularly in low‑income areas, buildings are in severe disrepair. Students speak of leaks, damaged ceilings, rats, broken toilets, insufficient furniture, and classrooms which overheat during recent heatwaves. 'It's either freezing in the winter or unbearably hot in the summer. The power cuts out, so the classrooms go dark, the computers stop working, the lights stop working' - Madeleine, high school student Class sizes are often overcrowded, reaching more than 36 students in urban areas, and school days are notoriously long. On top of this, around 10 percent of teaching hours go undelivered, with teacher absences hitting poorer areas hardest. "We have asbestos in the walls, classrooms where there aren’t enough chairs or desks. There are 35 of us in a classroom. We go to school from 8am to 6pm and then we have to do homework, it's impossible," a student from the Lycee Alfred Kastler in Pontoise, 30km northwest of Paris, told Middle East Eye. Other students criticised the lack of ventilation or air conditioning systems at school to battle surging heatwaves as well as repeated power failures. "We have major problems with insulation. It's either freezing in the winter or unbearably hot in the summer," Madeleine, a student at the Lycee Francois Villon in Les Mureaux, 40km northweast of Paris, told MEE. "The power cuts out, so the classrooms go dark, the computers stop working, the lights stop working. Nothing works anymore." Ousmane, 17, from the Lycee Emily Bronte in Lognes, an eastern suburb of Paris, said some classrooms don’t even have chairs. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); "Sometimes we have to stand during lessons," he told MEE. Other students mentioned the state of sanitary facilities in schools, saying that bathrooms are not cleaned, and reporting a lack of toilet paper and soap. In response to the protests, the government has acknowledged the "legitimate" nature of the grievances and pledged to address class sizes, daily schedules, teacher replacement mechanisms and building conditions. According to a Senate report, billions of euros will be needed in the coming years to renovate thousands of ageing schools. Banlieues suffer disproportionately While underfunding affects schools across France, those in deprived neighbourhoods with large immigrant populations are hit hardest. Unlike cities such as London, where different social and income groups as well has housing tenures are integrated within a single neighbourhood, Paris exposes a stark geographical divide, where wealth is heavily concentrated in the west and adjacent suburbs, while lower-income populations mainly live in peripheral northern and eastern banlieues. Criminalising protest: Pro-Palestine students in France face increased repression Read More » This contrast shapes students' experiences. According to the OECD, social background remains one of the strongest predictors of academic success, with disadvantaged pupils concentrated in under‑resourced schools where teacher absenteeism is higher and learning conditions poorer. Jelan Kone, a student from the Lycee Paul Eluard, one of the first high schools to have joined the protest movement, in the northern suburb of Saint-Denis, told MEE that racialised prejudices towards disadvantaged cities and their populations perpetuate institutional neglect. "They assume that because we’re from the banlieues, we’re supposed to be uneducated, that we don’t learn anything, that the suburbs are worthless," she told MEE. "But we don’t just let people walk all over us. We try to improve our communities and show that the banlieues aren’t something that should be neglected," she added. Mohamed, 17, who attends the selective Lycee International de L’Est Parisien in Noisy‑le‑Grand - one of the most disadvantaged cities in the Paris region, where 18.7 percent of residents live below the poverty threshold - stressed the importance of students from better‑resourced schools joining the movement. "It’s sad that others don’t have the opportunity to improve their social situation. It’s very important for us, in this area, to support neighbouring high‑school students out of solidarity," he told MEE at a mass protest in Paris’s Place de la Republique on Tuesday. 'They assume that because we’re from the banlieues, we’re supposed to be uneducated, that the banlieues are worthless' - Jelan, High school student Discrimination is also visible in the way police treat protesters, according to witness testimonies and extensive documentation of racial bias within French police forces. A 2025 study by the independent administrative authority Défenseur des droits (Rights Defender) found that young men perceived as Black, Arab or North African face a risk of identity checks four times higher than other population groups. Nellie, a high school student from the Lycee Alfred Kastler in the northwestern suburb of Cergy, told MEE police disproportionately target Black and Arab youth. "During one of the school blockades, I heard one student say to a policeman: 'I don't speak to cops'. The police man replied: 'We don't speak to Black people'," she said. Nellie's classmate Maelie told MEE that the police would "show up at their school, hit and tear-gas innocent people". 'No one listens to us' Another source of frustration among students is Parcoursup , France’s national higher‑education application platform. Students have raised concern over algorithmic biases in the system, saying that applicants from schools in more affluent neighbourhoods get prioritised, perpetuating already existing social and racial inequality. France: When racism peaks - and the mountains are claimed as white‑only spaces Read More » "We’re at a high school in the Paris banlieue. Because of that, we’re not viewed as favourably and it means that we don’t necessarily have the same opportunities as students from rich schools, even though we have the same level, and sometimes an even higher level than them," Imene, a high-school student in Saint-Denis, told MEE. "Parcoursup is a source of stress for all students in France. It’s unbearable. There are people who have an average grade of 18 out of 20 but were rejected by top universities, or from programmes like medicine, simply because other students were given priority," she added. Earlier this year, a Defenseur des droits report on discrimination based on origin among young people highlighted persistent inequalities in access to higher education and raised concerns about selection procedures, including Parcoursup. It called for stronger measures to ensure equal treatment and issued recommendations for Parcoursup to publish clear, verifiable and understandable selection criteria, strengthen ministerial oversight of admissions algorithms, and prohibit the use of applicants’ previous high schools as a selection criterion. Yet despite these calls for reform, many students say they still feel overlooked. Melissa, another high school student in Saint-Denis, told MEE that she feels that students, especially from the banlieues, are ignored by the government. "Everyone is equal in this country, we want to have the same rights as everyone else. That’s what they don’t want to understand. They just want us to stay quiet and put up with it," she said. 'We're not viewed as favorably and it means that we don't necessarily have the same opportunities as students from rich schools' - Imene, high school student Although many teachers support the protests, Imene, Melissa and Zara expressed concern over the socioeconomic gap between staff and pupils in Saint-Denis, which prevents them from relating to the students' grievances. "Most of our teachers studied at really prestigious universities. So for them, it’s not really the same experience. They don't come from the Paris banlieues, and they’re not racialised people," Imene told MEE. The protest movement, they said, will continue until the "students will be heard", arguing that students and staff have raised these issues for years without meaningful change. "Every single year, there’s another issue. But nothing changes," Zara said, deploring that despite the recurrent protests over the years, "no one listens to us". While speaking to MEE, Zara, Imene and Melissa were preparing for another blockade of their school on the following day, painting slogans on cardboards. More and more students joined them. Despite the violence and uncertainty, they expressed determination - and hope. "If we don’t act now, it’s never, ever, ever going to change. But this time, if we keep going, things will change, I have hope," Imene said. France Paris News Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:19 Update Date Override 0

Why this is no disaster for Polanski: Greens remain competitive as voters reward Burnham Submitted by Imran Mulla on Fri, 10/09/2026 - 10:21 The Green vote share surged to a historic high in Holborn and St Pancras, despite the party leader losing to Labour Green Party leader Zack Polanski reacts following the results in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, triggered by the resignation of Keir Starmer as MP, 9 October (Reuters/Toby Shepheard) Off Is this the end of Zack Polanski as leader of the Green Party? Many seem to think so - indeed, multiple national newspapers have suggested it. No doubt there are people in his party who want him out now he’s failed to be elected to parliament for Holborn and St Pancras. But on closer examination, Polanski’s defeat on Friday morning is far less of a catastrophe than many of his critics are claiming. The Green vote share surged to a historic high in the seat, and with a volatile electorate there are clear signs that the party can be optimistic about its potential for future growth. This is undeniably a victory for Andy Burnham. Labour’s candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali - with one of the most unusual backstories in British politics, as a child refugee from Somalia who enjoyed enormous success in local politics and rose to become leader of Camden Council - is locally well-known and popular. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ironically, Abdi-Wali is an ally of Keir Starmer, who she will replace in parliament, and her political positions have often seemed closer to Starmer’s than the new prime minister’s. Yet there’s little doubt that her win is in no small part a reflection of the "Burnham bounce" in the national polls. 'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference Read More » In the ethnically diverse Holborn and St Pancras, where the Gaza genocide remains a salient issue, many voters will have almost certainly wanted to reward the Burnham government for its recent sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements. Many voters, meanwhile, will simply be relieved that Starmer is gone and replaced by a more personable figure. Burnham is showing Labour can defend its seats and is clawing back votes it lost under Starmer. But this by-election won’t particularly embolden Labour strategists who are mulling an early general election next spring. The Green Party gave Labour a serious run for its money, with Polanski winning 8,928 votes (32.8 percent) to Abdi-Wali’s 12,292 (45.2 percent). Labour’s majority, just 3,364 votes, is extremely slim. By comparison Starmer’s majority was 11,572 votes in the 2024 general election, and even then his had been significantly slashed by independent candidate Andrew Feinstein. Remember that Holborn and St Pancras is historically a Labour stronghold. That status quo hasn’t exactly returned. Polanski has changed the party's fortunes Many in the Green Party see Polanski’s decision to stand for election during Burnham’s honeymoon phase as a significant miscalculation. In the short term this by-election will likely deal a heavy blow to the party’s momentum and image. But look at what the Greens have achieved in the past year. The party surged in the polls late last year after Polanski was elected leader. The Greens gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did. 'It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment' - Asma Alam, Green councillor Polanski is at least partially responsible for Starmer's downfall and Burnham's premiership. This means the Greens are now suffering from their own success. The party’s polling nationally has plummeted and is close to where it was in 2024. Crucially, however, in target seats - like London's Holborn and St Pancras - it is still performing strongly. It was never likely that Polanski could replicate the historic victory in Gorton and Denton, which mobilised both huge anti-Starmer sentiment and opposition to the visceral local threat of Reform. Yet Friday's was still the Green Party’s second best by-election result ever. Polanski has indisputedly changed the party’s fortunes. Hostile media “The result is really sad, but we always knew this was going to be a tight battle,” Asma Alam, a Green councillor and campaign coordinator, told Middle East Eye on Friday morning. “All this noise about new leadership needed is rubbish,” she added. “Zack won the leadership by a significant majority - that won’t change. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “It’s a setback, not doom. We are the biggest threat to the establishment.” Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told MEE at the party’s conference last weekend that "what we can continue to do is make sure that we’re holding the government to account". Ali added that if the Greens "are continuously providing better alternatives, the Labour government is going to have to take notice. "And if they don't, then we're waiting to sweep up their votes." The Greens have much to reflect on, including how the party can effectively deal with hostile media coverage, which will only increase. The by-election came after days of vociferous attacks on the Greens in the national media over the party conference vote last weekend to declare Zionism a form of racism. There is no evidence that anger over the conference vote played a role in influencing the by-election, but it is nonetheless likely that the barrage of hostile media coverage of Polanski and the Greens will have put off some undecided voters. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Everything to play for Significantly, the "Zionism is racism" motion, which dominated media coverage of the conference, involved Green activists, not the leadership, shaping the agenda. Polanski wasn’t even at the conference for the vote itself - he expressed discomfort with elements of the motion, although he said he thinks Zionism is racist - because he was campaigning in Holborn. Green Party recognises Zionism as a form of racism and backs single Palestinian state Read More » “I refute the idea that the motion impacted the results,” Alam said. “What it lost in potential votes it also added in votes from people who preferred our strong stance.” But Caroline Lucas, a former Green leader, has heaped criticism on Polanski, suggesting he failed to show leadership on the issue of the Zionism motion, which she strongly opposed. Will the Greens now seek to change the party’s internal system to give the leadership more control over the formulation of policy? This may be necessary for the party’s growth, but it would trigger a revolt among the membership. Internally, the Greens have tough questions which they need to resolve. Ultimately, though, the key lesson from Polanski’s performance in Holborn and St Pancras is that the electorate is still volatile. Since the 2024 election we have seen the implosion of the two-party political system. With Burnham in power, many pundits have prophesied its return. This has not happened yet, as the close competition in the by-election indicates. Depending on the Burnham government’s performance, support for the Greens could either plummet further or surge again. Voters are less loyal than they once were and no party can take them for granted. For both Labour and the Greens, then, there's everything to play for. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs398.96 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.72 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 9 (Friday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Direct shipping link with Europe restored. ISLAMABAD: Direct shipping connectivity bet­­ween Karachi and major European ports has been restored, providing relief to exporters facing longer transit times and incre­ased freight costs due to disruptions on international shipping routes, Federal Maritime Affairs Minister Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry announced on Thursday. In a statement, the minister noted that the Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) had “reinstated its PREMIUM IPAK service” in response to exporters’ demand for a dedicated and direct Europe service. Under the restored service, MSC will make wee­kly calls at Karachi Gate­way Terminal Inter­nat­ional (KGTI), connecting the port city to key Euro­pean destinations, incl­u­ding Felixstowe, Rott­er­dam, Hamburg, Brem­erhaven, Antwerp, Le Havre and London Gateway via Colombo. “Previously we had no tra­nsshipment service from Karachi Port. However, now we have a full-swing service as Pakistan has emerged as the transshipment hub of the region,” the minister said. He added that the restoration of a dedicated Europe service was an important development for the country’s export-oriented industries, particularly the textile sector, which had been facing increased transit times and logistics costs because of disruptions to international shipping routes. The minister referred to his meeting with textile exporters who had recently informed him about the difficulties caused by changes in shipping routes, particularly those linked to the situation in the Red Sea. “Exporters had earlier expressed concern that longer vessel journeys were increasing transportation costs and delivery times for shipments to European and US markets. These additional costs and delays have affected the competitiveness of Pakistani exporters,” he said. “The restored service will improve connectivity with major European ports and provide exporters with greater options for planning and moving their shipments,” he said. The minister, however, noted that the reinstatement of the service should not be viewed as a resolution of the wider challenges affecting international shipping routes. “Disruptions to established shipping routes continue to have implications for global trade. We will continue working with the shipping industry and exporters to address connectivity and logistics issues and to strengthen Pakistan’s position in international trade,” he said. Risk-based inspections In another development, the KPT chairman proposed standardised 24/7 electronic delivery orders, risk-based inspections, non-intrusive scanning, joint inspections and common sampling. He was chairing a meeting of the Working Group on Shipping Connectivity and Optimisation at the KPT head office, focusing on removing physical and regulatory bottlenecks and making cargo clearance faster and more predictable. Terminal operators exp­ressed readiness for night inspections, while Pakis­tan Customs was reques­ted to facilitate round-the-clock operations. Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

Saudis reel from attacks as allies debate ‘involvement’. • Houthis fire missiles at Riyadh airport, airbases; kindergarten, clinic complex damaged by debris • Lufthansa, Air India suspend flights to Saudi capital; half of all departures cancelled • Nothing in Makkah pact bars members from joining Yemen fight, says Kh Asif • Ankara calls accord ‘purely defensive’, rules out sending troops; Syria weighs deployment RIYADH: Yemen’s Houthi forces escalated their campaign against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that disrupted flights and damaged a kindergarten and medical complex. Lufthansa and Air India said on Thursday they will suspend flights to Riyadh as the Yemeni group renewed threats against airlines, after claiming a third attack on King Khalid International Airport. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, 49.7pc of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday across all Saudi airports. Flight tracker FlightRadar24 also showed numerous delayed arrivals and departures. The airport did not acknowledge the disruption, pointing only to the “necessity” of contacting airlines before travelling. A thick black column of smoke and flames rose from Riyadh airport in a video verified by Reuters . A witness and three people briefed on the matter said a stationary commercial plane had caught fire and caused the smoke, though the fire was later put out. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched two ballistic missiles at Riyadh’s airport, one at an airport in Najran and another at an airbase in Khamis Mushait. Saree also ordered workers at Saudi oil facilities to evacuate days after the group hit a major refinery south of the capital. Around the same time, the Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and another toward Khamis Mushait. Margaret Hamilton, scientist who worked on Nasa's Apollo program, dead at 90. American scientist Margaret Hamilton, who led development of the computer system used by Nasa’s Apollo lunar program, has died at the age of 90, her former employer said Wednesday. In a statement, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology called Hamilton, who taught at the prestigious university from 1959 to the mid-1970s, a “computing pioneer” and said she died on September 30. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” de Weck added. The famed Apollo program allowed the United States to beat the Soviet Union in the race to become the first humans to land on the Moon. NASA chief Jared Isaacman paid tribute to Hamilton on X, calling her “a pioneer whose work helped make Apollo and humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible.” Born in Indiana in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics before moving to Boston, Massachusetts with her husband in 1959. She found employment at MIT, working in meteorology before she joined a lab in 1965 that was seeking people to develop software to “send a man to the Moon.” Hamilton “was hired as the first programmer for the Apollo project at MIT, as well as the first female programmer in the project,” the university said. “By 1968, she was assistant director in charge of (Apollo’s) Command and Service Module team, and more than 400 people were working on Apollo’s software,” MIT said. ‘Pioneer’ Hamilton was credited with making critical onboard systems more robust and accident-resistant. Her software intervened approximately three minutes before the Eagle lander of the historic Apollo 11 mission touched down on the Moon, overriding a faulty script and ensuring the mission could safely continue, according to NASA. Jerry Wohletz, CEO of the Draper Laboratory — which was spun out of the MIT Instrumentation Lab — said Hamilton left “an indelible mark” on the company. “Through her leadership and contributions to the development of the onboard flight software for Nasa’s Apollo Guidance Computer, she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home,” he said. “We will honour her legacy at Draper forever.” Hamilton was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by former president Barack Obama in 2016 for her achievements. Then-US President Barack Obama presents mathematician and computer scientist Margaret Hamilton with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honour, during a ceremony honouring 21 recipients, in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC on November 22, 2016. —AFP/File In 2009, Hamilton told MIT News : “There was no second chance. We knew that. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s.” “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure. Dedication and commitment were a given. Mutual respect was across the board. Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” Hamilton added. “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers,” she said. Hamilton went on to publish more than 130 papers and started her own software companies Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.

US to livestream army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says. The US will livestream the army’s upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution. Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945. The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week. “It will be livestreamed. Details will follow,” a Pentagon official told Reuters , speaking on the condition of anonymity. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post. Media have sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, experts said. Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan . Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging of a young Black man who had been convicted of raping a white woman. Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1pm the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting was a “no-brainer.” “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public. Because people need to understand that… there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said. Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.” President must approve firing squad execution A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder. The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest. Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth’s recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday. The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon. The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan’s execution would be the first military execution since 1961. According to the Death Penalty Information Centre, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the centre reported. “It would be extremely, extremely strange” to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School. While firing squads have a long history in American military law, as far as he knew it would be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death. “The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it’s an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, ‘Well, it was OK in 1790, so what the hell?’” Fidell said. Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public. “What’s the point of it? Who would want to see that?” said Lurie. At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years. Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation. The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out. Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalised. Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke “angry and confused” in a hospital . Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

A wave of street protests, including in New Delhi, has attracted key leaders from India’s main opposition Congress party, including Rahul Gandhi, who was briefly detained during rallies this week. Protesters, including from the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, are calling for mass rallies in New Delhi on Saturday. Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in parliament, and other opposition leaders are expected to meet President Droupadi Murmu later Friday to complain about ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar. The ECI, India’s constitutional body responsible for conducting elections, has rejected allegations of wrongdoing. More than 20,000 police and paramilitary officers have been deployed in the capital ahead of the protest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported. Yellow metal barricades have sprung up across key roads in the city centre, restricting access to the government-designated protest site of Jantar Mantar, AFP reporters saw.
