Why India's tens of millions of voter deletions have led to widespread protests. India’s verification exercise of its nearly one billion voters has sparked protests across the country, with opposition parties alleging that the removal of 130 million names from electoral rolls has unfairly benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party. Opposition parties and the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party are demanding the ouster of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar and have vowed a huge protest ​in the capital, Delhi, on Saturday. Election Commission data cited by Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from ‌electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30m who could not be traced. The BJP and the Commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions. They say the deletions have affected the outcome of some recent state elections that the BJP won, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world’s biggest ​democracy. The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some reasons for their electoral dominance. Here are some details about the voter verification drive, which has become one of the biggest political controversies ​of Modi’s 12-year tenure ahead of crucial state elections starting early next year. What’s happening? Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party youth movement, farmers’ groups and opposition parties ⁠are set to protest in Delhi on Saturday, demanding the resignation of Kumar. Police say they have not granted permission, and CJP has reported preemptive detentions of some protest leaders. Sporadic protests have been going on across India ​since a report by the Indian Express newspaper in late September said Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems. The Commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, ​and has denied favouring any party. Demonstrators take part in a protest organized by opposition parties demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in Ahmedabad, India, on October 8. — Reuters Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Why does it matter? At least seven Indian states will hold elections next year, including BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, the most populous and considered a bellwether state in national politics. Verification in Uttar Pradesh began in October 2025 and resulted in 13 per cent of names being deleted, according to local media reports. Voters with their names missing need to prove their credentials ​before being enrolled, and many have complained about the process. Verifying a billion voters: the controversy India started verification of its voter rolls last year ahead of elections in the eastern state of Bihar, ruled by a BJP ​coalition. The review has now covered the majority of Indian states. While voter roll revisions are routine, this round became controversial after large numbers of voters in states such as Bihar and West Bengal found their names missing from electoral ‌rolls and were ⁠unable to cast ballots. The BJP won power in West Bengal for the first time in May. Citing Election Commission data, the BJP says that of the 130m names deleted from voter lists, 28m are dead, 63m have relocated, 10m are duplicates and 30m could not be traced by officials. Opposition parties, including Congress, have accused Kumar of bias and alleged that the process benefits the BJP, charges the Election Commission and the party deny. The Indian Express story said the two deputies to the election commissioner had expressed concerns to Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, but those concerns were not taken into consideration. The Election Commission said all its decisions ​were lawful. The report prompted opposition leaders and members of ​the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party, which in July forced ⁠the education minister to quit after weeks of protest, to launch nationwide demonstrations. Demonstrators break the barricade as they protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, in Patna, India, on September 28, 2026. — Reuters What happens to voters removed from the rolls? The Election Commission says names are only removed when a voter has died, is mentioned more than once on the rolls, has moved to another region or is untraceable. Officers are required to record detailed reasons why a voter ​is deleted. People whose names do not appear in draft rolls can request inclusion before final voter lists are published and also raise appeals if such ​requests are denied. Voters excluded from ⁠final rolls can also challenge the decision. To participate in future elections, excluded voters must succeed in their appeals or apply for fresh registration. Opposition parties argue that arbitrary deletions and lengthy appeals prevented millions in Bihar and West Bengal from voting and could be used as a weapon in future elections. Election commission’s defence The Election Commission has defended itself from allegations of political bias, including at a rare press conference by Kumar last year, who asked the opposition to submit ⁠their allegations under ​oath. Kumar has had a difficult relationship with opposition parties since taking over as the election body chief in February 2025. Opposition ​lawmakers put forward a motion to have him removed earlier this year, but it was rejected by parliament. Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) attend a protest demanding women’s safety in Bengaluru, India, on October 8, 2026. — Reuters A 2023 law passed by Modi’s government grants the election commission chief immunity from prosecution for acts done in an official capacity. Amid the recent backlash, the Election Commission announced revisions ​to the verification process, including home visits by officials to collect documents and an extension of the deadline for final verification in some states.

Malaysia closes schools in capital, parts of country due to haze. Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday, as haze from fires in neighbouring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst. Toxic smoke from peatland as well as forest fires has shrouded towns and cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing. The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting. Kuala Lumpur’s air quality worsened on Friday to hit a reading of around 224 on the index of Swiss-based monitor IQAir, which said that change pushed Malaysia’s capital past Singapore to be the “most polluted global major city”. Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed full school closures in four states and two federal territories as well as one partial closure in the central Pahang State. Schools were also closed on Friday in three districts in western Perak State. Malaysia’s education ministry could not immediately be reached for comment on whether schools will reopen on Monday. “In the future, we will ensure that any decision to close schools is notified in advance so that parents have sufficient time to prepare,” Fadhlina said late on Thursday. Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API). “Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said. Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency. ‘Necessary steps’ Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday he discussed the fire situation with the Indonesian leader Prabowo Subianto. “The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo,” Anwar said. “And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” Anwar said, without going into specific details. He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding. Indonesia’s government said “regular dialogue between the leaders is a natural part of the close relations” of the two nations. Experts said the flames are being fanned by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon , causing the worst pollution conditions in years. Anwar said he asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter. “So these are all the steps we are taking, but we are monitoring and will try the measures that we ought to take next,” Anwar said. Singapore’s air quality levels too dipped into the “very unhealthy” range with a reading of 209 on the AQI in Friday afternoon, according to the IQAir website. The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks. Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.

PM Shehbaz condemns fresh Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reiterates commitment to kingdom's security under Makkah pact. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to the Gulf state’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” under the Makkah Defence Alliance. The defence pact , of which Turkiye is also a part, was signed on August 7 and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. In a post on X, the premier condemned attacks targeting Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, noting that the attacks had resulted in civilian casualties. He also commended the “vigilance and professionalism” of the Saudi armed forces and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen for intercepting ballistic missiles. PM Shehbaz expressed “unwavering” solidarity with Saudi Arabia. “In line with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and recent decisions taken by its Strategic Political and Defence Committee, our commitment to the Kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security is resolute,” he said, adding that Pakistan fully supported Saudi Arabia’s right to self-defence. He called on the Houthis to immediately cease attacks. “We will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Saudi Arabia in the face of these threats.” On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that they had struck the Saudi capital’s main international airport with a ballistic missile, in the latest attack on the kingdom claimed by the group. The attacks came after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom and are targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Both sides have claimed strikes on each other as tensions remain high. On Wednesday, Saudi authorities said three people were killed and 36 injured in attacks on two of the kingdom’s international airports, including in the capital, Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. For its part, a Saudi-led coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it “destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform” used in the attack on Riyadh. The Houthis, who control most of the country’s northwest, are battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and they captured swathes of coastal land. Yemen’s internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and said Houthi fighters were pushed out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha. But the Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On October 5, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and was asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, to which he said both Turkiye and Pakistan had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

Vatican envoy commends Pakistan's constructive role in promoting regional peace, stability through mediation: FO. Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s secretary for relations with states and international organisations, on Friday commended Pakistan’s “constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability through mediation, dialogue and diplomacy”, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The archbishop is visiting Pakistan to mark the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Pakistan and the Holy See. In a statement, the FO said that Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar received Archbishop Gallagher at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. FM Dar welcomed Archbishop Gallagher and acknowledged the Holy See’s role in “promoting peace, interfaith harmony and dialogue”, the FO said. The foreign minister also appreciated the valuable contributions of Pakistan’s Catholic community, particularly in education and health, it added. According to the statement, Archbishop Gallagher commended Pakistan’s “constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability through mediation, dialogue and diplomacy”. Moreover, FM Dar appreciated Pope Leo XIV’s principled calls for peace and a just resolution of the Palestine conflict and reaffirmed Pakistan’s unwavering solidarity with the Palestinian people, the FO stated. During the meeting, they expressed “deep concern over the continuing humanitarian crisis and emphasised the importance of sustained international efforts to advance peace in the region”. “Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening Pakistan – Holy See relations and promoting mutual respect, understanding and peaceful coexistence among faiths,” the statement concluded. In an earlier statement, the FO said that the visiting archbishop was also expected to meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Meanwhile, Archbishop Gallagher is also expected to interact with members of the Catholic community while in Pakistan. “The visit marks an important milestone in the longstanding relations between Pakistan and the Holy See and reflects their shared commitment to further strengthening mutual understanding, cooperation and trust, while promoting interfaith harmony and peace,” the FO added.

DG ISPR says Pakistan acting as an ‘honest broker’ in US-Iran war. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said Pakistan is acting as an “honest broker” while mediating between the United States and Iran, reiterating the commitment to a “negotiated and peaceful” outcome. The military’s spokesperson made the remarks in an interview with CNN correspondent Ivan Watson, who posted a small clip of the interview on his X account. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked whether Pakistan can “still play a neutral role [in the US-Iran war] when Iran has targeted Saudi Arabia in the past, with the Makkah alliance , and now you have an Iranian ally — the Houthis — attacking Saudi Arabia”. “Can Pakistan be a neutral broker?” Watson asked. In response, Lt Gen Chaudhry said: “Pakistan has been exhibiting that we are a very honest broker … everything stems from honesty. We have been very clear on where Pakistan stands with all our partners”. He recalled that when the US-Iran war began, Pakistan had openly condemned Israeli attacks on Iran and also condemned Iran’s retaliatory campaign in the Gulf. “So we have been honest about that. We don’t mince our words; we have a stake in regional peace and stability. We tell all that nobody benefits from expanding this war,” he said. Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan was committed to a “negotiated and peaceful” outcome to the conflict. He stressed that the country was doing “whatever is possible, whatever is necessary so that the gap narrows”. “We want that the conflict should not expand horizontally or vertically.” In a small clip of the interview released on Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about deployment of Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia under the Makkah defence alliance. In response, he said Pakistani troops were in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. In a longer clip of the interview posted by state-run Pakistan TV on X on Friday, the military’s spokesperson said that such questions were dwelling on the operationalisation of the force. “The Makkah accord, its actualisation and whatever effects it achieves, that will be purely defensive. That’s how the partners, that’s how the principles have agreed, that’s how it is going to manifest itself,” he said. “How that will be done, which component will go there, how it will be employed, that’s for the operational commander to decide. And the operational details, because it’s a military conflict … no participating country starts disclosing how and where I am going to employ my forces,” he said. “So how and when they will be employed, you will see [for] yourself,” he said. However, Lt Gen Chaudhry hastened to add that it would be “defensive in nature”. He went on to say that under the United Nations charter, all countries had the “right to self-defence”. “It is best, that rather than the threat [manifesting] into an actual operation or a military conflict, you ward it off through collective deterrence,” he said. He went on to say that the signatories of the Makkah defence pact, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, had potent military and diplomatic capabilities. “So, then anyone who is having some funny ideas against any other will hopefully think twice, thrice or multiple times. So, that stops something terrible [from] happening. That is how collective deterrence works,” he said. The remarks by the military’s spokesperson come amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and as the US-Israeli war on Iran, in which Islamabad has been playing the role of a mediator, shows no signs of abating. Meanwhile, the defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Monday, the three countries agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of alliance in Riyadh.

Archaeologists discover ancient structure at Jandial in KP near Sirkap. A previously unstudied, ancient structure measuring nearly 100 metres long and 50 metres wide has been discovered at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Khanpur-Taxila region. The discovery has opened “new avenues for understanding the history and urban landscape of Gandhara”, a press release said on Friday. The monument, identified as Jandial D, lies opposite the famous Ionic temple of Jandial , outside the ancient fortified city of Sirkap. First noted by Alexander Cunningham in 1864, the structure remained largely unexplored for more than a century. Workers dig at the excavation site at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. —Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Excavations that began in mid-August 2026 revealed substantial walls, while the monument’s precise function — whether public or religious — remains under investigation. The discovery was made by the KP Archaeology Department under the Khyber PATH Project, directed by Italian archaeologist Dr Luca M. Olivieri and funded by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS). The project is being implemented by the Italian Archaeological Mission of Ca’ Foscari University of Venice in collaboration with the KP Directorate General of Archaeology and Museums. It is supervised by KP Director General of Archaeology and Museums Dr Abdul Samad. Italian NGO ISCOS provided logistical and financial support for the project. Workers dig at the excavation site at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. —Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Dr Abdul Samad said the discovery highlighted the archaeological potential of the Khanpur–Taxila region and the importance of continued scientific research and international collaboration, stressing the need to protect archaeological remains threatened by expanding urbanisation. He said, “The discovery at Jandial demonstrates that the archaeological landscape of KP continues to hold important historical secrets. “Our priority is to support scientific research, strengthen international partnerships and protect these irreplaceable heritage assets.” Khyber Path Director Dr Olivieri said the discovery demonstrated the “richness and unpredictability of the region’s archaeological landscape”. “Its monumental scale and strategic location raise important new questions about the ancient landscape of Sirkap and the wider Gandharan region.” The Khyber PATH project has been ongoing for a year at eight archaeological sites across KP from Swat to the Khanpur–Taxila region. Its work includes the excavation and conservation of ancient fortifications at Sirsukh and research at Bazira/Barikot, which is on UNESCO’s Tentative List .

Navi Pillay, head of UN commission that declared genocide in Gaza, wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Navanethem “Navi” Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” the Norwegian Nobel Committee said. Pillay held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict, and demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career, the committee said. “A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the committee said. “This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo. The Nobel jury said it was honouring her at a time when “the system of international law is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”. “At a time of existential challenges — including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time — international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity,” Watne said. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said. Pillay was chair of the United Nations Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that concluded last year that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report as “scandalous”. The prize — the ultimate diplomatic and humanitarian accolade — is sure to irk US President Donald Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize. “If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump,” Pillay said to a standing ovation captured by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on the social network X. The peace prize is the fifth Nobel awarded this week, after literature, chemistry, physics and medicine. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado won in 2025. The Nobel Peace Prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns, or about $1.2m, is due to be presented in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will. Pakistan nominates Trump Shortly before the announcement, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif took to X and said Pakistan had nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his role in “advancing peace in South Asia”. Referring to last year’s brief military conflict with New Delhi, the prime minister said Trump’s “timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire that is holding till today”. “In recognition of his outstanding contribution, Pakistan had nominated President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize,” he added. “We sincerely hope the president’s efforts to promote peace and prevent conflict in our region receive due recognition this time,” he said. Last year, the government had decided to formally recommend Trump for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for his “decisive diplomatic intervention and pivotal leadership” to end the India-Pakistan escalation in May. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked with Pakistan. Islamabad strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation . After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed five Indian planes in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight . After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire . Since then, the US president has praised both PM Shehbaz and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir on several occasions. Most recently, he called PM Shehbaz a “terrific man” during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month.

Bilawal, Rana Sana made members of Judicial Commission of Pakistan. ISLAMABAD: PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and Adviser to the Prime Minister Rana Sanaullah on Friday were made members of the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP). Two seats in the JCP were vacant after the recent resignations of PPP stalwart Senator Farooq H. Naek and PML-N member Aftab Sheikh. Both Bilawal and Rana will represent Parliament as members of the treasury benches in the respective Houses – the National Assembly and the Senate. The nominations were made by Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif, who is also leader of the House in the National Assembly, as well as Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Senator Ishaq Dar, who is the leader of the house in the Senate, under Article 175A (2)(vii) of the Constitution. A notification for the appointments was issued on Friday by the JCP with the approval of Chief Justice of Pakistan Yahya Afridi, who is also the body’s chairperson. The next JCP meeting is scheduled for Oct 13, when the body will meet to consider extending the term of the Sindh High Court’s Constitutional Benches. The JCP is mandated by the Article 175A of the Constitution to appoint judges of the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), the Supreme Court, the high courts and the Federal Shariat Court. The commission also evaluates the performance of the judges of the high courts. Under the 26th Amendment , changes were made to Article 175A, which reconstituted the JCP with the inclusion of four members of parliament — two each from the treasury and opposition, one from the National Assembly and the other from the Senate. The commission consists of chief justices of the SC and the FCC, the next most senior judge from each court, and two judges from each court jointly nominated by the chief justices for a period of two years. It also comprises the federal law minister, the attorney general for Pakistan, an advocate with no less than 15 years of practice in the SC, two members from the Senate and the National Assembly each from the treasury and opposition benches, and a woman, non- Muslim or technocrat other than a member of the Parliament, who is qualified to become a member of the Parliament.

Short-term inflation rises to 11.97pc, PBS data shows. ISLAMABAD: Short-term inflation rose to 11.97 per cent year-on-year in the week ending Oct 8, driven largely by higher food prices , particularly wheat flour, according to official data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) on Friday. The Sensitive Price Index (SPI), which tracks short-term inflation, rose 0.57pc week-on-week, reflecting price fluctuations in both food and non-food items. Of the 51 essential items monitored during the week, prices of 20 commodities (39.22pc) increased, while those of six items (11.76pc) declined. Prices of 25 items (49.02pc) remained unchanged from the previous week. Short-term inflation has remained in double digits for several consecutive weeks, largely on the back of persistent increases in petroleum prices. Unwilling to ease the petroleum levy , the government has continued to raise petrol and diesel prices on a daily basis. The surge in energy costs is not only fuelling inflationary pressures but also indirectly boosting sales tax collections through higher prices of goods and services. According to tax analysts, higher inflation benefits the government in terms of increased sales tax collection. Meanwhile, an unprecedented increase in transportation costs has also been reflected in the prices of essential food items, including onions, tomatoes and other vegetables. Chairing the National Price Monitoring Committee (NPMC) meeting on Thursday, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal expressed concern over rising prices of essential commodities, particularly wheat flour, and directed provincial and district administrations to strengthen monitoring of supplies, market arrivals, hoarding, profiteering and unjustified price increases. This is cost-push inflation, in which rising energy costs are followed by increases in food prices. As a result, households are under pressure from higher consumer prices. The items whose prices increased the most over the previous week included wheat flour (5.69pc), chicken (4.93pc), pulse gram (3.99pc), petrol and tomatoes (2.40pc each), pulse masoor (1.29pc), prepared tea (1.08pc), cooked daal (0.98pc), pulse mash (0.91pc) and LPG (0.57pc). The items whose prices declined week-on-week included bananas (2.81pc), diesel (1.37pc), potatoes (0.89pc), sugar (0.37pc), gur (0.19pc) and pulse moong (0.03pc). On an annual basis, the items that recorded the highest price increases included onions (100.24pc), LPG (68.55pc), electricity for Q1 (58.59pc), petrol (47.52pc), diesel (42.52pc), wheat flour (32.60pc), chilli powder (15.55pc), mutton (15.02pc), beef (12.60pc), chicken (9.44pc), plain bread (8.99pc) and curd (8.08pc). In contrast, potato prices fell by 39.51pc, followed by tomatoes (37.07pc), sugar (22.44pc), eggs (18.88pc), powdered salt (14.81pc), pulse masoor (9.79pc), gur (8.59pc) and pulse moong (8.37pc). The index, which comprises 51 items whose prices are collected from 50 markets in 17 cities, is calculated weekly to track changes in the prices of essential commodities and services. The data shows that the prices of 20 items increased, six decreased and 25 remained unchanged from the previous week.

PIA temporarily suspends flights to Riyadh citing ‘situation in the Middle East’: spokesperson. Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) on Friday temporarily suspended its flight operations to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, citing the “situation in the Middle East”, according to a spokesperson. The suspension comes amid regular drone and ballistic missile attacks on Riyadh and other airports in Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthi militia, as fighting between Saudi and Houthi forces intensifies. PIA asked passengers to contact its call centre to check the latest status of their flights before leaving for the airport. Meanwhile, 104 flights arriving at or departing from Riyadh airport were cancelled and 154 were delayed on Friday, according to Flightradar24. The website’s data showed that 335 flights had been cancelled on Thursday. Flightradar24 shows the lack of flights arriving or departing from Riyadh airport. — Screenshot Flightradar24 The Pakistan Airports Authority also confirmed that PIA had suspended flights to Riyadh, clarifying in a statement that other than that, flight operations to Saudi Arabia continued as usual and “speculations circulating on social media are not true”. PIA’s decision follows similar moves by several other airlines, including Lufthansa Group and three Indian carriers, which suspended flights to Riyadh on Thursday. A Lufthansa spokesperson told Reuters that the German group’s airlines would suspend flights to the Saudi capital until October 16, citing “current developments in the Middle East”. India’s largest airline, IndiGo, said it had cancelled all flights to and from Riyadh until October 9. Air India and Akasa Air also told Reuters that they had cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital until October 10. Yemen’s Houthi forces escalated their campaign against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that disrupted flights and damaged a kindergarten and medical complex. A thick black column of smoke and flames rose from Riyadh airport in a video verified by Reuters . A witness and three people briefed on the matter said a stationary commercial plane had caught fire and caused the smoke, though the fire was later put out. After loud booms echoed across Riyadh on Thursday morning, several multinational firms in the King Abdullah Financial District told staff to work from home or evacuated employees, according to people familiar with the matter. Diplomats were instructed to shelter in place at their embassies, and at least one international school sent children into a basement for safety. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched two ballistic missiles at Riyadh’s airport, one at an airport in Najran and another at an airbase in Khamis Mushait. Saree also ordered workers at Saudi oil facilities to evacuate days after the group hit a major refinery south of the capital. On Wednesday, three people were killed in attacks on two Saudi international airports including in the capital Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to the Gulf state’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” under the Makkah Defence Alliance. The defence pact , of which Turkiye is also a part, was signed on August 7 and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Pakistan, along with Turkiye, on Monday agreed to deploy military forces and capabilities rapidly in Saudi Arabia. Soon after the US-Iran war began, PIA suspended flights to several Gulf countries on March 1, including United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait. At the time, the airline said it would not suspend flights to Saudi Arabia.

Navi Pillay — South Africa's global rights activist and Nobel winner. Former UN rights chief Navanethem “Navi” Pillay — awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday — is a global rights defender who has also served on the International Criminal Court and was South Africa’s first non-white woman high court judge. The 85-year-old built a formidable reputation during a decades-long career that took her from South African courts to the ICC and the International Tribunal for Rwanda. She gained global prominence for her outspoken condemnation of government repression of popular protests in the Arab world, including Libya and Syria. Between 2021 and 2025, she chaired a commission of enquiry created by the UN Human Rights Council to probe the root causes of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The panel, which does not speak for the UN and has faced harsh Israeli criticism, found that “genocide is occurring in Gaza and is continuing to occur”, Pillay told AFP in 2025. “The responsibility lies with the state of Israel,” she said. Pillay is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, working on a case deciding whether Myanmar’s crackdown on the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, with a ruling expected in the coming months. Groundbreaking Born the daughter of a bus driver in South Africa’s east coast city of Durban in 1941 to a family of Tamil descent, Pillay has had a groundbreaking career. She grew up in a poor neighbourhood in the southeastern coastal city during white minority rule, and studied law at the University of Natal before attaining a Master’s and Doctorate from Harvard. She became the first non-white woman to open a law firm in Durban where she carved out a reputation as a doughty defender of apartheid opponents. An illustration depicting 2026 Peace Prize laureate Navanethem “Navi” Pillay is pictured after, after the announcement of the 2026 peace prize winner, in Oslo, Norway on October 9, 2026. In 1973, she won the right for political prisoners in the notorious Robben Island penal colony — where jailed anti-apartheid leader Nelson Mandela was held at the time — to have access to lawyers. A year after Mandela became president in South Africa’s first democratic vote in 1994, she made legal history by becoming the first woman of colour to be appointed to the country’s high court. Soon after, the late liberation hero recommended her to serve on a United Nations tribunal trying Rwandan genocide suspects. In 1998, she was among judges on the Rwanda tribunal that was the first to try rape as an act of genocide. Ten years later, Pillay was appointed UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, a role she held until 2014. Voice of victims Her upbringing in an unjust apartheid society spurred her to fight discrimination everywhere and earned her the reputation of being the voice of victims around the world. “We put up with the worst insults and racial discrimination and abused and treated like dirt,” Pillay told AFP in an interview in 2023. That could have made you “weak and cry” or “fight every step of the way”, she said. “So I always had a sense of confidence about who I am and how you confront any kind of discrimination. Open your mouth and speak up, condemning it. And that’s what I did in the UN.” The rights defender married in 1965 lawyer Gaby Pillay, who was also a political prisoner she represented while he was tortured in detention during apartheid rule. The couple divorced and Gaby died in the late 1990s. They had two daughters.

Moscow disagreement. THE fact that a consensus on how to deal with terrorism originating in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan eludes regional states was made clear at the recently held Moscow Format moot. The event was attended by nearly all of Afghanistan’s neighbours, including Pakistan. However, there was no joint statement issued because, in the words of the Russian envoy for Afghanistan, “our Afghan and Pakistani colleagues didn’t see eye to eye”. The Taliban regime had also sent its representatives. The main sticking point was the Taliban’s objection to including Afghanistan in a “terrorist context”. However, as Pakistan’s envoy put it, it was essential to address “the menace of terrorism emanating from Afghan soil”. Russia offered its good offices to help de-escalate matters between Kabul and Islamabad, though it noted that the Moscow Format was not a forum for resolving bilateral disputes. Both the Taliban’s denialism, and Russia’s apparently soft stance towards the Afghan terrorism problem, are unfortunate. Groups that find shelter in Afghanistan under the Taliban threaten the entire region. Thus, all of Afghanistan’s neighbours need to speak with one voice regarding the ‘export’ of terrorism. Russia is the only state that recognises the Taliban regime. Moscow has its own reasons for indulging the Taliban; these include the need to fight IS-K, which is a common enemy of Russia and the Taliban rulers, as well as to check US and Western influence in Afghanistan. But engagement with Kabul must not be allowed to obscure the fact that some of the deadliest terrorist groups in the world find refuge on Afghan soil. Other regional forums, such as the SCO and the ECO, have highlighted the need to address the terrorist threat emanating from Afghanistan. China, which has significant economic interests in Afghanistan, has also pointed to this terrorist threat. The UN Security Council , too, has frequently noted that Afghanistan under Taliban rule has once again become a haven for various terrorist groups. Pakistan’s insistence, therefore, that Afghanistan’s terrorism problem be highlighted reflects the reality of the situation. If Kabul addresses the issue sincerely and restrains terrorist groups, it will benefit not only the Afghan people but the entire region. Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

Azeri woman’s gang-rape case: Lahore court extends physical remand of two prime suspects by four days. LAHORE: A judicial magistrate extended on Friday the physical remand of two prime suspects by four days in an Azeri woman’s gang-rape case . The two prime suspects, arrested of the three accused in the case, were produced before Judicial Magistrate Azhar Mahmood at the Cantonment Courts following the expiry of their remand period. The case has been registered with Defence-C police on Sept 26 on the complaint of a 20-year-old Azeri woman, who had travelled to Pakistan for business purposes and was allegedly gang-raped by three men in a rented flat of a private housing society located near Raiwind. During the hearing on Friday, the investigating officer (IO) told the court that a substantial part of the investigation had been completed, but the police still needed to recover the suspects’ mobile phones. The IO sought an extension of their physical remand to recover their phones and complete the investigation. The magistrate accepted his request and extended the suspects’ remand by four days. The case Apart from the three prime suspects, the complainant has also accused two women of abetting the crime. One of them is on physical remand with the police while the other is on bail. On Sept 27, the complainant recorded her statement before Judicial Magistrate Muhammad Sagheer under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). In her statement, she said she had arrived in Pakistan from Istanbul on Sept 13 and travelled to Lahore after staying in Faisalabad for five days. She said she had contacted two women to meet her in Lahore and later accompanied one of them to a house in Bahria Town, where she met the other. The group subsequently moved to an apartment, where three men allegedly raped her. The woman alleged that one of the men locked her in a room and the suspects refused to let her leave unless she drank alcohol with them. She said the men later threw her out of a car at an unknown location, threatened her against approaching the police and took her handbag containing Rs200,000 and two mobile phones. She also alleged that one of the women had taken Rs20,000 to Rs30,000 from a suspect, while both women were present during the events leading to the alleged assault. It is the second such case in which a foreign woman has been allegedly gang-raped in Lahore’s Defence-C police station area during the last four months. In June, two foreign women, nationals of the Netherlands and Venezuela, were allegedly abducted and sexually assaulted in the Defence-C police station area. According to the FIR, the women were abducted by five suspects, including a close relative of a senior political personality, who demanded ransom and subjected them to sexual assault during their captivity.

Pakistan handed Twenty20 International caps to all-rounders Razaullah and Imran Randhawa as Sri Lanka won the toss and elected to bat first in the opening fixture of the three-match series at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Friday. Both Razaullah and Imran made their Test debuts in the third and final Test against England last month. It was the former, however, who made it a memorable outing for himself, scoring a quickfire 81 in Pakistan’s second innings after having taken four wickets in the first. The Sri Lanka series marks Sahibzada Farhan’s first assignment as Pakistan’s full-time T20 captain after leading the national side at the recent Asian Games, where Pakistan won a silver medal after losing to India in the final. The 30-year-old opener, who has played 48 T20Is, said on Thursday that he was excited about leading Pakistan on home soil and confident that the new combination could produce results. “This is the first time I am representing my country as a captain. It is a great honour for me,” Farhan told reporters at a pre-series press conference. “There is pressure, but it is not that we will let that pressure sit on our heads.” He said his experience of leading domestic sides and the Asian Games team had prepared him to handle the demands of captaincy. Farhan’s elevation is the most visible sign of a wider change in Pakistan’s T20 setup. Established names Babar Azam, Mohammad Rizwan and Shaheen Shah Afridi are absent, while Salman Ali Agha has also been removed from the T20 leadership group. Farhan, however, said the doors remained open for senior players. “Babar and Rizwan are experienced players and have remained among the world’s best. Diegograndi Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 8 minutes Updates from the UN General Assembly 2026 Marking the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly, Crisis Group experts discuss challenges facing the UN’s efforts to promote international peace and security. This page includes updates from the High-Level Week in New York and recent Crisis Group coverage of the UN. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy World leaders are gathering in New York during the week of 21 September for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. They will find an organisation trapped in an open-ended institutional crisis. UN diplomacy to halt wars and ease civilian suffering is largely paralysed, while a second year of cost cutting has weakened the organisation’s capacity to respond. The UN is in need of revival. Even with these limitations, the UN remains the only universal forum for international cooperation on war and peace, even as the world order it anchors is under mounting strain. Many member states hope that the next Secretary-General, set to be selected by the end of 2026, can help the organisation forge a new direction that enhances diplomacy and deepens respect for international law. A new Secretary-General, regardless of the skills and experiences that she or he may bring to the role, cannot solve the world’s crises overnight. But she or he can and should work with member states to address immediate challenges. High on the list should be bolstering the UN’s peacemaking and conflict management capacities, mobilising political and financial support, and making a renewed case for international cooperation. This special coverage page will feature all of Crisis Group’s work related to the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week in 2026, as well as its broader work on the UN from the past year. The New Forever War mloukili Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:38 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 1 minutes The New Forever War Originally published in Foreign Affairs Why America and Iran Fight On Without Victory Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Ali Vaez Deputy Program Director, MENA https://twitter.com/AliVaez Related Tags Iran United States When will the war in Iran end? American officials claim that the answer is soon. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the [November] election,” declared U.S. President Donald Trump in September. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Iranian leaders agree that the war’s conclusion is near. Tehran has “brought the most heavily armed army in the history of the world to its knees,” proclaimed Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in August. Many outside analysts think that the conflict will drag on for longer and end with negotiations rather than with a clear winner. But generally, there is a sense that the fighting will soon be resolved, one way or another. Such thinking is understandable. All wars eventually end, and after months of rising energy prices, the world is especially eager for this one to stop. Yet the unsettling reality is that the conflict is nowhere near over. The war’s two principal belligerents cannot achieve their desired goals, yet they both feel they are accomplishing enough to make continued fighting through a mix of military and economic tools worth it. The United States cannot topple the Iranian regime, get it to give up its missile program, force it to abandon its nuclear program, or make it stop supporting its regional partners. But Washington can keep degrading Iran’s military and constricting its economy. Iran cannot evict the world’s only superpower from the Middle East. Yet it can keep damaging U.S. regional bases, bombing the United States’ regional allies, and disrupting international commerce. The full article can be read on the Foreign Affairs website. South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 11:07 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 29 September 2026 2 minutes South Sudan’s President Jettisons Unity Government and Hardens Grip on Power Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech examines how President Kiir’s call for fresh elections aims to weaken his opponents, and may pave the way to worsening armed conflict Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Daniel Akech Senior Analyst, South Sudan https://twitter.com/jongethon Related Tags South Sudan South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir on 22 September dissolved the transitional unity government, established under a 2018 peace deal, declaring that the country would now prepare for long-delayed elections in December. But with the feasibility of holding the polls in doubt and fighting between government and rebel forces continuing in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, the move in effect serves to further concentrate power in the hands of Kiir and his family. Kiir’s move followed the adoption by parliament, which is loyal to the president, of a controversial amendment to the National Elections Act on 21 September, authorising the creation of a caretaker government. This amendment gave Kiir the opportunity to remove his five vice presidents – many of whom were appointed under the 2018 deal, including his perennial arch-rival, First Vice President Riek Machar. The government had already placed Machar, who led the rebel forces in the five-year civil war that ended in 2018, under house arrest in March last year, charging him with treason . State and rebel forces have been fighting since then, threatening to thrust South Sudan back into internecine conflict. Its last civil war is estimated to have cost nearly 400,000 lives and displaced more than four million people. President Kiir further marginalised rival factions and opposition elements in his caretaker government. His newly appointed ministers are almost entirely loyalists, whereas the Nuer – South Sudan’s second-largest ethnic group, to which Machar belongs – remain heavily underrepresented. There are now three Nuer cabinet ministers out of a total of 17, even after the president added additional appointees on 28 September. Kiir also appointed powerful figures from the security forces to become caretaker governors in key states, such as James Koang Chuol in Upper Nile, Moses Majok Gatluak in Jonglei and Rin Tueny Mabor in Lakes. Some political leaders have denounced the unrepresentative make-up of the new administration and rejected the changes. Kiir’s moves set up two potential scenarios. One is a rush to stage-manage snap elections, the first of their kind since the country’s independence in 2011, which could end up re-electing Kiir despite questions as to whether credible polls are even possible without an updated census, voter registry or dedicated funding. A mismanaged vote could also spark fresh rebellions or political violence. Alternatively, Kiir could delay elections yet again on technical grounds, effectively extending his term without the baggage of the 2018 accord’s power-sharing arrangements. Kiir is using an “inter-party dialogue” that started on 24 September to validate plans for elections in December or negotiate such an extension. Either way, Kiir’s moves have triggered alarm among the South Sudanese political elite that his aim is to consolidate power with the goal of managing a dynastic succession . His daughter Adut Kiir is now his most powerful aide, while his son Atem Salva Kiir oversees the presidential guard. Meanwhile, the new rebellion by Machar’s forces looks unlikely to subside as long as its leader remains on trial and under arrest. The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? eschelhaas Tue, 09/29/2026 - 18:14 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Iraqi security forces stand guard during a funerary procession for a slain member of Iraq's Hashed al-Shaabi, or the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), who was killed in a US-Israeli air strike in Mosul the previous evening, in Baghdad on March 8, 2026. AHMAD AL-RUBAYE / AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 29 September 2026 14 minutes The U.S.-led Anti-ISIS Coalition is Leaving Iraq: What Happens Next? The coming withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces marks a significant moment in Iraq’s tumultuous recent history. Yet with the Middle East war bringing conflict to the country and questions surrounding the state’s capacity to assert its authority, the significance is mainly symbolic. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Also available in Arabic English Arabic Related Tags Iraq United States On 30 September, the U.S.-led coalition formed to fight the Islamic State (ISIS) is due to end its military mission in Iraq. While some had expected that the withdrawal of personnel and removal of materiel might slip beyond the scheduled date, it now appears that they will be completed on time. The largest remaining contingent is from the United States, which has maintained the biggest troop presence throughout. Several other coalition countries already have pulled out their smaller garrisons, including Poland, which completed its drawdown in March, and Germany , whose soldiers left in August. The departure closes a chapter that began in 2014, when ISIS seized large parts of the country and U.S.-led forces – which had previously invaded and occupied Iraq in 2003 and then withdrawn in 2011 – returned at Baghdad’s invitation. A number of Iraqi armed groups that first formed to combat ISIS came to cast the coalition as a threat. Aligned with Iran, these groups long invoked the coalition’s presence as a justification for keeping weapons and command structures outside the Iraqi state. With coalition forces on their way out, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has declared that these groups must now disarm. But the coalition is leaving amid a Middle East war sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, in which Tehran and some of its aligned groups based in Iraq have launched attacks on U.S. targets in Gulf Arab countries, Jordan and Iraq’s own Kurdistan region. The question is whether Baghdad can and will use the end of this foreign military mission to gain greater control of armed actors who – whatever justification they may offer – have reasons for fighting that extend well beyond opposition to the coalition’s presence. The End of a Mission The U.S.-led Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria – dubbed Operation Inherent Resolve by the U.S. military – is ending its mission twelve years after its establishment. At that time, in 2014, a marauding ISIS had capitalised on the instability that gripped much of the Arab world following the 2011 uprisings, helped by the acquisition of conventional weapons from Iraqi and Syrian forces that quickly retreated from major cities such as Mosul and Raqqa in the face of the group’s onslaught. It exploited growing sectarian tensions in Iraq and perceptions of political exclusion among its Sunni Arab population to seize much of the country’s Sunni Arab heartland. In June 2014, ISIS declared a caliphate in Iraq and Syria and at its height, in May 2015, controlled as much as a third of Iraqi territory. Having terminated the U.S. occupation of Iraq only three years earlier, then-U.S. President Barack Obama decided to send troops back to prevent ISIS from expanding further and reverse its gains in both countries. In the ensuing years, the U.S. and dozens of coalition partners supported military operations against the group in both Iraq and Syria at the same time as they sought to help rebuild and train the Iraqi army, which had collapsed in a matter of days after the ISIS offensive. While the Iraqi government declared victory over ISIS as early as December 2017, having retaken Mosul and other key cities from ISIS control and secured its border with Syria, the coalition endured. It remained in the country even after March 2019, when the final ISIS stronghold in Baghouz, Syria fell; that loss marked the end of the group’s control of the last bit of the territory it had grabbed since beginning its 2014 offensive. The coalition – which included sizeable contingents from France, the UK and Türkiye in addition to the U.S. – stayed on for several reasons. First, it continued to support Iraqi armed forces suppressing residual ISIS cells for years after the recapture of Baghouz. The Iraqi army and Kurdish region’s armed forces ( peshmerga ) continued to suffer occasional hit-and-run attacks in the so-called disputed territories, an area claimed by both the federal and regional governments, whose rugged terrain offered ISIS fighters plenty of hideouts. As late as August 2024, U.S. troops operating alongside Iraqi forces sustained injuries during a raid on an ISIS cell in Anbar province. Secondly, the coalition used Iraq as a base from which to conduct operations against the group and others across the border in Syria, where a civil war raged for years, and where the U.S. partnered with the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) until April. The ISIS danger appears to have significantly receded. Despite occasional attacks by its remnants, the group has lost its ideological traction. Though some people in both Iraq and Syria continue to harbour the grievances that ISIS played upon to galvanise support, few want to relive the era of the so-called caliphate, which triggered years of conflict and destroyed many of the communities the group ostensibly sought to protect. Moreover, the security gaps that ISIS exploited in 2014 have also narrowed in both countries. Syria’s new authorities have yet to establish full control of the country’s provinces and borders, but the process of integrating the previously autonomous SDF in the north east under the central government’s command is helping secure areas that remain vulnerable to ISIS. In Iraq, state forces are better prepared to repel any domestic or external threat the group might pose. Though the coalition and the Iraqi government share the assessment that Iraqi forces can counter ISIS on their own, the withdrawal is also politically expedient for both Baghdad and Washington. For years, despite its cooperation with coalition forces, Baghdad viewed their presence as a liability, not least because Iran-aligned armed groups seized on it to claim that the U.S. occupation was continuing. Those groups also accused the U.S. of using its foothold in Iraq to monitor Iran and the “axis of resistance” – its partners in the region. This latter charge became a justification for the Iraqi groups to retain their arms and command structures independent from the Iraqi state forces. Domestic political dynamics on the U.S. side may not have been as clear-cut, but they nevertheless militated for withdrawal. Trump was never the pure non-interventionist that he seemed to tout himself as being, but he has long sounded off against the Iraq war (a key theme of his 2016 campaign) and had already considered withdrawing from Syria during his first term. Despite his growing penchant for military intervention in his second term, Trump has continued to inveigh against endless U.S. wars, notably in the Middle East. Departing from Iraq is thus consistent both with the president’s longstanding rhetoric and also the views of significant parts of his political base. To the extent that Washington had contended that the coalition remained in Iraq at its government’s request, Baghdad’s desire for a troop withdrawal has for some time been a complication. Lastly, as a U.S. official noted to Crisis Group, amid the war with Iran, withdrawal would have the added benefit of reducing readily accessible U.S. targets for Tehran. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. In theory, the withdrawal should mark a milestone in Iraq’s relationship with the U.S. and its long road to normalcy following the chaos and violence that have plagued the country since the 2003 U.S. invasion. A series of Iraqi governments have desired to forge bilateral security cooperation agreements on Iraq’s own terms and with countries of its choosing. Baghdad can now strike these deals, not only with the U.S., but also with other former coalition partners such as the UK and France. But however politically necessary it may have deemed the withdrawal, Baghdad will hardly be able to sell the coalition’s departure as a celebratory moment, given that it coincides with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has turned Iraq into a battleground. Instead, the withdrawal’s timing will focus further attention on that conflict’s spillover effects. Unlike during the 2011 U.S. withdrawal, Iraqis need not anticipate the next war; it is already affecting the country. The fears of many Iraqis are therefore presently not centred around the risk of a resurgent ISIS but rather around Iran-aligned domestic groups that, in solidarity with their “axis of resistance” partners, and notwithstanding the U.S. withdrawal, may take action in defiance of the government’s policy of neutrality in the U.S.-Iran war, and thereby provoke military retaliation by outside actors. Some of the complications that the withdrawal could present for the Iraqi-U.S. relationship would have been difficult to anticipate when the drawdown timeline was conceived. That happened at another tense moment, following the outbreak of the Gaza war, when U.S. backing for Israel’s brutal military response to Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attacks undermined public support for bilateral close ties. In September 2024, when Zaidi’s predecessor Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani was prime minister and Joe Biden was U.S. president, Baghdad and Washington agreed on a phased end to the coalition’s military mission. It would start with the coalition’s withdrawal from bases in federal Iraq by September 2025, to be followed by the final withdrawal from the Kurdistan region by the next 30 September. Now, with the U.S.-Iran war as backdrop, the withdrawal may well attract less attention as an indicator of the country’s recovery from ISIS than as a test of whether its government can repair Iraq’s battered sovereignty and protect its internal security at a moment of regional crisis. Reining In Armed Groups Zaidi has declared that the end of the coalition mission should mark the beginning of disarmament for groups that operate independently of the state. He has set June 2027 as the deadline for its completion. His political argument is straightforward: once the coalition troops are gone, the armed factions should no longer be able to invoke their presence as grounds for maintaining separate military structures. As he announces the mission’s conclusion on 30 September, he is expecting some of the factions to welcome a development that meets their longstanding demand and to reciprocate with their own commitment to cease hostilities. But not all of the armed groups will do so, given the variations among them and the dynamics created by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The Popular Mobilisation Forces, or Hashd al-Shaabi, emerged as a collection of Shiite armed groups assembled to fight ISIS and were subsequently nominally incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus, with many retaining independent chains of command. They do not form a single faction and have very different relationships with Tehran. Not all have engaged in attacks outside Iraq’s borders. Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq, appear willing to negotiate their future relationship with the state. Others, including factions associated with the self-described Islamic Resistance in Iraq, such as Kata’ib Hizbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, are tied ideologically and operationally to Iran’s regional network. Their opposition to the U.S. extends well beyond the presence of coalition troops in Iraq, and they have served as a valuable vector for Iranian power projection. It is these latter factions that have participated in the Middle East war, striking U.S.-linked targets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries, including Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Their actions have strained Baghdad’s relations with Gulf states and, as noted, exposed Iraq to military retaliation by both the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Zaidi thus has good reasons of his own to want to curb them, as his government cannot credibly reassure its neighbours, attract investment or pursue a foreign policy of neutrality while armed actors make decisions on war and peace independently of its will. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. Negotiations under way with individual groups offer a possible, albeit incremental, pathway to bringing personnel and capabilities under state command. They also are almost certain to take far longer than Zaidi’s deadline allows. If the talks stall, Zaidi could face U.S. pressure to use force against groups that earlier prime ministers were reluctant to confront militarily, fearing an intra-Shiite conflict and friction with Iran. In a mid-September interview , Zaidi said groups continuing to function as separate militias would be considered outlaws. He has yet to specify what action the government would take to corral those that defy him. As long as Tehran relies on close Iraqi partners in its war with the U.S., these groups have reason to preserve their military autonomy and may seek to prolong negotiations without relinquishing their arms. Even after the coalition’s withdrawal, they will likely point to other foreign security relationships, including Türkiye’s garrison in northern Iraq, to defend their stance. Some have also argued that any disarmament plan must simultaneously address the status of the Kurdish region’s peshmerga, although the parallel is inapt: peshmerga forces are governed by a specific law under the Iraqi constitution regarding federal regions’ responsibility to organise their own internal and border security. The government therefore ought to distinguish between forces operating under recognised state or regional authority, and factions conducting attacks without any such justification. The Kurdish Region’s Vulnerabilities The coalition’s departure has particular significance in the Kurdistan region, where its forces have supported the peshmerga and where U.S. troops remained even after leaving other bases in Iraq in September 2025. Erbil is not happy to see them depart. Regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani described withdrawal at this moment as “ shameful ”, no doubt because he is concerned about how to manage the threat posed by Iran and Iran-aligned groups, which have systematically targeted the region since the war began in February. Some of the strikes appear to have been motivated by the presence of U.S. forces, in line with attacks on other nearby countries hosting U.S. bases. But the near-daily strikes also have often hit Iraqi-based Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and were described by a Kurdish official to Crisis Group as a warning to Kurdistan to keep those groups out of the current conflict. Certainly, the coalition’s withdrawal will exacerbate vulnerabilities. Coalition forces based in Erbil provided the region with some level of air defence. Their impending departure will mean the loss of those capabilities, further exposing the region to missile and drone attack. The Kurdish official noted to Crisis Group that worries about the withdrawal were “not just about security and protection, but the message this sends to our adversaries”, reflecting fears that Iran and others will see the U.S. drawdown as an indication that they would no longer take a significant interest in the region’s future. Still, U.S. support will not necessarily dry up entirely, even if the basis for it will change. To date, U.S. support for the peshmerga has been governed by a memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs, first signed in 2016 and last renewed in 2022 . But though the U.S. does not wish to extend the agreement, Kurdish authorities will continue to press Washington and other coalition partners for aid in the form of strikes, intelligence sharing, training and equipment – none of which necessarily requires a troop presence inside Iraq – as well as broader reassurance of assistance in facing the military threat from Iran and the groups that it backs. It may help that the regional government announced in September its completion of a peshmerga reorganisation sought by the U.S. and agreed to in the lapsing memorandum. But future cooperation will require further work to define the terms on which Baghdad, Erbil and foreign partners will operate. Erbil and Baghdad, whose relationship has traditionally been fraught, will surely have to work together more closely. That said, at least for now, Kurdish officials say they are impressed with Zaidi and believe he is sincere in his stated intention of trying to tackle the militia problem. Looking Ahead When Trump returned to the White House for his second term, much of his base hoped and believed that his administration would avoid military adventurism and seek to extract the country from strategic quagmires. Some of his personnel decisions, particularly at the Pentagon, seemed to lend credence to such speculation, as did the foreign policy views of his vice president, JD Vance. Officials who sought to pursue a more restraint-oriented foreign policy or to concentrate on competition with China by downsizing other overseas commitments were not a dominant force within the new administration but nevertheless held key positions. Both of these groups favoured reassessing U.S. force posture in the Middle East, particularly the legacy missions in both Iraq and Syria. Whatever influence these camps have, their perspectives have not guided key foreign policy decisions in Trump’s latest year in office, which has been characterised by aggressive unilateralism and reliance on military force as a tool of statecraft. But the trajectory of U.S. policy on Iraq and Syria is an exception to that trend. Administration sources tell Crisis Group that, buoyed by the unexpected ouster of President Bashar al-Assad in Syria, key U.S. officials, particularly at the Pentagon, pushed to reassess the U.S. troop presence there and prevailed in a series of internal policy debates on the matter. Those efforts were boosted when it became clear how vulnerable U.S. troops in the region had become as a result of the conflict with Iran. U.S. officials also have positive views of Zaidi, who visited Washington in July and was received warmly by Trump. They are particularly pleased by Zaidi’s pledges on armed group disarmament. Even those who are sceptical of how those efforts will fare appreciate the Iraqi prime minister’s tone and confidence. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. What comes next for U.S.-Iraq relations will likely depend on the uncertain trajectory of the U.S. war with Iran. A prolonged conflict is likely to lead Iran to enlist its partners in Iraq to use the country as a staging ground for significant attacks on the interests of the U.S. and its regional partners. That in turn would inevitably undermine the bilateral relationship and could trigger retaliatory U.S. moves at a time when Washington still enjoys outsized influence, including because it controls a significant portion of Iraq’s oil proceeds, which are deposited in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Trump administration has already twice used the leverage the oil revenue affords the U.S. in pressing Iraq to take more proactive measures to dilute Iran’s influence. For now, Zaidi’s ascension has eased strains, and the U.S. withdrawal gives him an argument for reining in armed groups. That may be enough for him to make progress with some of the groups, but doubters are right to question how far he will be able to go. Indeed, it would be entirely unrealistic to expect that Baghdad can compel the surrender of weapons or severing of ties with Iran forged through years of regional conflict. The symbolism of 30 September is significant, but in the end Iraq’s stability will depend more on whether the U.S. gives it the time and space required to bring armed groups under its central authority, and whether Baghdad and Washington work together to protect Iraq from the worst effects of the U.S.-Iranian confrontation in the meantime.
